The router's MediaTek MT7996 radio captures raw 14-bit IQ at up to 320 Msps, its Airoha AN7581 SoC streams it over 10 GbE, and a Linux host shows it as a live spectrum and waterfall in the browser, with the receiver's controls next to it. The whole 2.4 GHz band at 320 Msps, live, with the decimation's roll-off corrected in the stream ("flatten"): a 262,144-point FFT of every sample, 100 spectra a second (this recording runs at 50 frames a second). The MT7996 runs only our own firmware: a ROM patch, WM and WA built from this repository, with no MediaTek code. It brings the radio up from a cold power-on by itself, from MediaTek's initialisation and calibration decoded register by register against a trace of MediaTek's own firmware, and takes its commands (LO, sample rate, capture, stream, gain, filter) from the host. See docs/architecture.md and docs/roadmap.md . What it does Sample rates 40, 80, 160 or 320 Msps of 14-bit complex IQ on every band, independent of the LO and the filter; on band 2 also 640/2 (every other sample of 640 Msps: flat to ±155 MHz, but signals 160–320 MHz away fold in) Bands 2.4 GHz (MT7976), 5 GHz and 6 GHz (two MT7977s); switching bands is a register write inside a running stream Tuning No channels: the LO is any Hz a band's synthesizer locks at (unit A: 2.081–2.748, 4.647–7.509 and 4.707–7.576 GHz), on its grid of 2.98 Hz (2.4 GHz) or 11.9–14.3 Hz steps; retuned mid-stream (about 1 ms) Front end AGC or manual LNA/baseband gain; analog filter 20–320 MHz Transport the radio DMAs into a 1 GiB ring in SoC DRAM; the kernel sends every 8 KiB slice as one UDP datagram, zero-copy, on the 10 GbE port; at 320 Msps half the slices are packed to 28 bits per sample pair on the radio's own cores to fit the link (lossless, automatic) Host w1700k-stream receives the export and serves the IQ stream to every consumer on the host (shared memory, complex int16, gap-tagged), with an optional correction ("flatten") of the decimation's roll-off applied to the samples themselves; w1700k-spectrum : 262,144-point FFT at 100 frames/s over every sample, browser UI, live controls; sdr-recv records the stream Screenshots 2.4 GHz at 320 Msps, flattened: Wi-Fi frames and shorter hopping bursts on a floor that stays level to the band's edges. The Stream panel shows the link carrying 9.75 Gbit/s, half of the slices packed, and every sample transformed. Two busy 80 MHz Wi-Fi channels at 5170–5330 MHz in a flattened 320 MHz view. Zoomed to 24 MHz around 5250 MHz: the two channels' edges and the guard gap between them, in 1.22 kHz bins. Repository Path platform/ What runs on the SoC: our U-Boot, Linux 6.18 with board patches, a read-only BusyBox root kernel/w1700k_sdr/ The MT7996 driver (firmware download, the DMA ring, the 10 GbE export, the firmware's command mailbox) and its unit-side clients firmware/ Our MT7996 firmware: the ROM patch, the WM (radio bring-up and band set-up, streams, RF control) and the WA (packer) host/w1700k/ Host control: firmware load, streaming, RF control as firmware commands; w1700k serve for the web UI host/stream/ w1700k-stream , the host's one receiver of the export: the IQ stream in shared memory for every consumer, and the roll-off correction host/spectrum/ The spectrum/waterfall web server host/recv/ sdr-recv , the stream recorder init/ Installation from stock, updates, recovery include/hw/ Register reference: every known MT7996, A-die and AN7581 register, as C headers docs/ Architecture , roadmap Getting started You need a W1700K, a 3.3 V USB serial adapter on its console header, an Ethernet cable to its lan3 port for installation, and a 10 GbE NIC on the host cabled to its wan port (10GBASE-T; an X710 with a copper SFP+ module works) for the IQ stream. make # everything, from public sources (~10 min plus downloads) make check # the test suite sudo init/host/link up IFACE # 192.168.1.10/24 on the NIC cabled to lan3 sudo init/host/tftp-forward enable IFACE init/install # back up the NAND, install, save the radio calibration sudo init/host/link up IFACE10G 10.77.0.10/24 9216 # the 10 GbE stream link host/stream/build/w1700k-stream & # the stream, for every consumer on this host host/spectrum/build/w1700k-spectrum --controller " host/bin/w1700k serve " --listen 0.0.0.0:8073 Then open http://HOST:8073/ and press ▶. The first start loads the radio firmware and brings the radio up (about 2 s). Without the browser, the same operations are host/bin/w1700k load|start|band|tune|gain|filter|stop|status . Build requirements: a C/C++ compiler, make, git, Python 3.10+, the usual Buildroot prerequisites, clang, ld.lld, llvm-objcopy and llvm-readobj (RISC-V firmware), openssl (firmware container encryption), and libfftw3-dev and zlib for the stream service and the spectrum server. No vendor firmware is downloaded or needed. Read before use Our firmware is receive-only. It runs none of MediaTek's transmit calibrations and keeps the MAC's transmit path disabled; a gapless watch at 5250 MHz saw nothing during a load, where MediaTek's firmware transmits a full-power burst. Still, do not cable an antenna port straight into a sensitive instrument without an attenuator. Our ROM patch writes no eFuse. MediaTek's ROM patches since 2025 permanently program one eFuse gate bit on their first run (also with MediaTek's own driver); a unit that ever ran one has that bit set. Installation replaces the stock operating system. init/install first copies the whole NAND to the host; keep that copy. Restoring stock needs a raw NAND writer, which this repository does not provide. Accessing undocumented MT7996 or AN7581 addresses can hang the SoC or wedge the radio until a power cycle. include/hw/ marks every known hazard. Licence MIT, except the Linux driver and kernel patches (GPL-2.0-only), U-Boot patches (GPL-2.0+), the driver's user-space header (GPL-2.0 WITH Linux-syscall-note) and files derived from MediaTek's mt76 driver (BSD-3-Clause-Clear). title: A Modern Web App in C
body_text: A modern web app in c | Corey Prophitt # Corey Prophitt Â» A modern web app in c ## INTRO If you wanted a dynamic website in 1994, you wrote a C program, dropped it in a cgi-bin directory, and let Apache fork it per request. Thirty-two years later, I shipped a commercial web product using fundamentally the same technology. Everything about marketyour.games is modern. It's a web product with user accounts, a search dashboard for content creators, folders for organizing them, payments via Stripe and transactional emails via Postmark. It follows progressive enhancement and doesn't require any JavaScript. Everything is modern except the way it was made and how it is served. Here are my thoughts on writing a real product in C and serving it via CGI in 2026. ## TLDR CGI's decline was justified in 2004 but doesn't hold up in 2026. You can write a modern web application in C. I shipped one. One binary, a SQLite file, three dependencies and the entire thing fits in your head. ## HOW IT WAS DONE The stack is BCHS : OpenBSD, C, httpd, and SQLite. There's no framework. You write a C program that reads CGI environment variables and responds. There's no templating language. You write C that outputs the HTML directly. There's no separate database server. You open the database file through SQLite's C API. There's no container. You build a statically linked binary and drop it in a folder. Every request spawns a fresh process. Deploying a new version is replacing one file. That means no server restart and no downtime. New requests simply pick up the new binary. OpenBSD ships with sane defaults and gives you the tools to actually secure a C program like pledge and unveil. Httpd serves from a chroot by default, so your CGI binary runs sandboxed to its own corner of the filesystem. I lean on three additional libraries: libcurl handles all outbound requests to Stripe and Postmark. libsodium handles random identifier generation, password hashing and the HMAC verification for Stripe webhooks. libcjson handles JSON parsing for Stripe and Postmark. Only two of those are actual build dependencies: libcurl and libsodium. libcjson is a single C file and has no external dependencies. SQLite ships an official amalgamation (single C file) build. Both are vendored and built as part of the project. The result is a build with almost no moving parts. A clean build takes a few seconds and rebuilds complete in less than half a second. Instead of serving static assets the traditional way, I route all traffic from httpd to the CGI binary. Every asset is compiled into the executable and served from memory. ## WHAT I LIKED Fundamentals over frameworks. CGI isn't a framework to learn. The 1.1 specification was published in 2004 and hasn't changed since. There's no API to internalize. The entire interface is a handful of fundamental HTTP concepts: Request headers. Request methods. Query strings. Body data. If you understand HTTP, you already understand CGI. It's language and platform agnostic. You learn it once and the knowledge is good forever. Clear separation of concerns. A modern web application typically puts a web server like nginx in front and reverse-proxies to an application server written in another language like Ruby, Python, Go, or Rust. That always felt a bit strange to me: you essentially have two web servers, and one of them is also responsible for your business logic. CGI gives you a single web server that calls your business logic directly. It's clear who does what. It makes debugging simpler, too. Your application is an ordinary program you can run from a shell: pipe it a request, watch stderr, step through it with gdb. In a sense, CGI resembles serverless architecture: a supervisor invokes your code per request, hands it a bag of environment variables, and collects the result. CGI is serverless, minus the vendor (and surprise bills). Minimal supply chain risk. With the rise of autonomous agents and weekly attacks on package repositories, it feels reassuring to have very few dependencies. Most modern tech stacks come with a package manager and an ecosystem to go along with it. It's convenient, but the dependency graph balloons. One or two direct dependencies can pull in hundreds of indirect ones, each maintained by somebody you've never heard of, with publish credentials protected by a password reused since 2015. My supply chain is a C compiler and three libraries. Compromising it would require compromising libcurl... a project the entire internet watches, not a package with eleven weekly downloads and an owner who left in 2019. Simple tooling. I'm a minimalist at heart. I use classic Vim with zero plugins. That means no LSP, no autocomplete, no code formatters, and no AI. Complex tech stacks demand complex tooling: they demand a language server to wade through the layers of abstraction. But this stack is simple enough a plain editor is all you need. The entire application is a directory of C files and a Makefile. Open a file, read it, and you know what it does. Great tooling is within reach. When you do want tooling, it's not far. Sanitizers, valgrind, gdb, ctags, cscope... these are mature (well, geriatric) tools that have been refined for decades and they're a package install away on any system that can compile C. The maturity goes further than the tools themselves: integration is built into many editors. Vim ships with native support for ctags, cscope and has a graphical gdb frontend (see :h Termdebug). Writing HTML and CSS in C isn't too bad. I was hesitant to write the entire frontend in C, but it wasn't nearly as painful as I imagined. All too many times have I: Fought vim to highlight Go's html/template syntax. Fought helix to detect Go templates without breaking html detection. Fought rustrover to recognize jinja templates for a project using askama. Using C means there's no second language for your editor to half-detect, no mixed-syntax where highlighting falls apart, no plugin dance to get the two languages to cooperate. It was refreshing to just write C. It isn't pretty, but neither is Tailwind. SQLite is a breath of fresh air. I've always defaulted to Postgres for web applications. It's a great database, but it comes with some operational burden. There's a server process to babysit and frequent releases to upgrade to. SQLite has none of that. There's no process, no configuration, no dependencies. Your application opens the database file directly. The operational burden is minimal. ## WHAT I WOULD CHANGE CGI is an interface between a web server and your application. There's no framework or library. This means you get very little out of the box. You need to write your own utilities to handle things like: Cookie parsing and creation. Query parameter parsing and validation. Form data parsing and validation. Escaping input for display. I rolled my own in a single header file (cgi.h), but I'm not convinced that was the right solution. Libraries like kcgi exist, but adopting one means buying into its API and security model. I'd like to see a set of shared utilities that developers can drop in (like the stb libraries). Maybe I'll publish cgi.h as a start. ## CONCLUSION CGI is old, but it's not forgotten. Most of the reasons we abandoned it in the early 2000s don't hold up today. Process forking isn't nearly as expensive as it was; modern kernels optimize it heavily. And if the cost of forking ever became an issue, FastCGI is a simple enough upgrade. Writing a modern web application in C is more than feasible— marketyour.games is a commercial product running on a single binary using a serving model that was officially standardized in 2004. It has fewer moving parts than anything I've shipped before. I'll be reaching for this stack again.

Trending RAM Combo Deals Surface Laptop Ultra with RTX Spark RAM Shortage AI Data Centers Vera Rubin Nova Lake AI Chip Design Week Tom's 30th Anniversary Tech Industry Cybersecurity 'Unprecedented' Cyberattack cripples supermarket fridges across Europe as hackers activate automatic defrosting  — delivery and store prices also impacted by incident News By Stephen Warwick Published 12 October 2026 France, Belgium, and the Netherlands are reportedly affected. When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works . (Image credit: AFP) Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Reddit Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article 14 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter An ongoing cyberattack has reportedly struck major supermarket chains across Europe, disrupting refrigeration control systems. The attack — which has reportedly seen units set to continuously defrost at 50 degrees Celsius — is also apparently affecting deliveries and in-store pricing powered by electronic shelf labels, La Dépêche reports . According to the report, "several" major retailers have been targeted by a cyberattack, which has hit Danfoss-made refrigeration controls used by French supermarkets Intermarché, Leclerc, and Coopérative U. Indeed, the latter's president, Dominique Schelcher, has confirmed as of Monday morning that "A cyberattack has been affecting the refrigeration production facilities of several stores in our network since last night." Schelcher said teams had been mobilized to fix the issue and promised an investigation into the incident, which he described as "extremely serious." Je confirme qu’une cyberattaque touche depuis cette nuit les installations de production de froid de plusieurs magasins de notre réseau @CooperativeU. Nos équipes sont pleinement mobilisées, en lien avec les frigoristes, pour rétablir la situation au plus vite. Une enquête devra permettre de faire toute la lumière sur cette attaque. S’attaquer à des équipements essentiels à la conservation des produits frais et à l’approvisionnement alimentaire des Français est d’une extrême gravité et est inédit. C’est inacceptable. October 12, 2026 The report states the units have had their automatic defrosting systems activate, but that hackers have also configured the function — which normally runs for just two hours a day — into a continuous, forced defrosting cycle with the temperature set to a toasty 50 degrees Celsius. Sources reportedly described "a wave of heat" escaping from fridges and freezers Latest Videos From Tom's Hardware Watch full video here: Early reports indicate losses are already approaching 300,000 euros, but could run into several million euros nationwide. Separately, NOS in the Netherlands reports that several supermarket chains have been hit with a malfunction due to a cybersecurity incident on Sunday afternoon. Albert Heijn, Etos, and Gall & Gall have had their websites taken down, impacting deliveries. Electronic shelf labels have also been compromised, disrupting in-store pricing. "We have immediately taken measures to protect our IT environment. Part of this involves the preventive temporary shutdown of a number of systems," Albert Heijn said in a statement. It is unclear at this stage whether the two attacks are related or how widespread either of them is. Belgium's Delhaize chain, which belongs to Albert Heijn, has also reported disruption. Images online show stores in Amsterdam warning customers about price problems, and the suspension of loyalty programs that have also been impacted by the incident. As for smart TVs, just buy one and dont connect it to wifi and dont plug in a lan cable Reply bit_user jp7189 said: Monitoring, logging, alerting, and control of temps that directly correlate to spoilage and lost revenue.. yeah.. cant see any reason a multinational supermarket chain would want that... /s But there's a difference between passive monitoring vs. the ability to do remote control. Clearly, the potential for exploits didn't factor into somebody's calculus, when they decided to add features for remote control. I hope the short-term fix is simply to power-cycle the fridges and disable their online connectivity. title: Citroen revives the 2CV for an electric age
body_text: Citroen revives the 2CV for an electric age Skip to content Watch Live British Broadcasting Corporation Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Home News US & Canada UK UK Politics England N. Ireland N. Ireland Politics Scotland Scotland Politics Wales Wales Politics Africa Asia China India Australia Europe Latin America Middle East In Pictures BBC InDepth BBC Verify Sport Business World of Business Technology of Business NYSE Opening Bell Technology Watch Documentaries Artificial Intelligence Intelligence Revolution AI v the Mind Tech Now Health Watch Documentaries Culture Watch Documentaries Film & TV Music Art & Design Style Books Entertainment News Arts Watch Documentaries Arts in Motion Travel Watch Documentaries Destinations Africa Antarctica Asia Australia and Pacific Caribbean & Bermuda Central America Europe Middle East North America South America World’s Table Culture & Experiences Adventures The SpeciaList To the Ends of the Earth Earth Watch Documentaries Science Natural Wonders Climate Solutions Sustainable Business Green Living Audio Podcast Categories Radio Audio FAQs Video Watch Documentaries BBC Maestro Discover the World Live Live News Live Sport Documentaries Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live Citroen revives the 2CV for an electric age 1 day ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Theo Leggett International Business Correspondent Stellantis French carmaker Citroen has brought back its 2CV brand in a bid to boost sales of electric cars in a difficult market. The new model, unveiled at the Paris Motor Show, is a small city runabout with retro styling which harks back to one of the company's most famous designs. As a "concept car" intended to show Citroen's direction of travel, it is not yet ready to go on sale but the plan is to have a version in showrooms by 2028. As they face mounting competition from Chinese manufacturers, Citroen and other European brands are exploiting their heritage as a means of selling modern motors. Farmers’ favourite Citroen chief executive Xavier Chardon described the new car as "a modern, ingenious and refreshing response to the mobility challenges of tomorrow". The original Citroen 2CV was launched in 1948, as Europe was recovering from the ravages of World War Two. It was designed as a cheap, robust way for French farmers and country folk to get around. The car had high wheel arches and soft suspension, letting it travel across a ploughed field or rough roads - as legend would have it, without breaking a tray of duck eggs. Its high roof let drivers wear a hat at the wheel. It was easy to drive and simple to repair. The car was so popular, it remained in production for more than 40 years. Over time, it went from being a utilitarian tool for the countryside to a cult classic, and a favourite of hippies and counter-culturalists. Getty Images Fans of Citroën's 2CV hold annual meet-ups such as this muddy gathering in Switzerland Now, Citroen wants to draw on that heritage to sell an electric, small city car that is expected to sell for about £13,000. The look of the new 2CV may well evolve as Citroen develops its design. But as it stands, it shares plenty of styling features with its famous predecessor. The high, flared wheel arches, the tall, curved roof and the eye-like headlights are all reminders of the original "deux chevaux" or "two horses". By using memories of an old car to sell a new one, Citroen is following a well-travelled road. VW notoriously brought back the Beetle in the late 1990s, with limited success. BMW's Minis have always carried styling designed to hark back to the very British original. Fiat has been selling a retro-styled Fiat 500 for the past two decades. Retro-nostalgia But the retro-nostalgia trend has accelerated recently, as carmakers have looked for ways to sell electric cars to sceptical consumers. Citroen's French rival, Renault, has led the charge. It started with the Renault 5 E-Tech, which visually echoed the distinctive boxy styling of the original Renault 5, once an ever-present sight on French streets. It has since revived the Renault 4 and Twingo brands as well. VW has the distinctive ID-Buzz minivan, a throwback to the classic T2 Transporter, while Ford is working on a new EV which is widely expected to be called the Fiesta. Rachel Burgess, senior editor of Autocar magazine, thinks it is a strategy that makes perfect sense. "It's a brilliant differentiator from all-new car brands", she says. "An older audience might remember the originals and feel warmly towards them, and a younger audience might find an appeal in the retro aspect." Finding new ways to make cars appealing has become more important than ever, at a time when European manufacturers are facing growing competition from Chinese brands. "Many in the industry believe the big automotive players in Europe…face a very serious existential threat from aggressive Chinese manufacturers," says David Leggett, automotive editor at Global Data. Getty Images Back to the future: VW looked to the past when designing its ID-Buzz minivan In this hostile business environment, heritage and nostalgia could prove to be powerful weapons for more established brands, thinks automotive researcher and author Dr Paul Nieuwenhuis. "In a world where a wave of credible decent quality Chinese EVs are hitting Europe, linking European designs back to their history while using the latest powertrain technology is something the Chinese cannot do," he says. "The Chinese can establish new design trends, but there is limited history there." But Leggett thinks Citroen will need more than a heady whiff of nostalgia to turn its new car into a best-seller. "A reimagined Citroën 2CV should give a big nod to its ancestor - especially on price and design simplicity as well as visual cues," he says. "But it also needs to be a credible modern electric car in terms of functionality and features, with widespread appeal." title: GLM-Legal
AI is a tool and using it well takes skill
body_text: AI Is a Tool. Using It Well Takes Skill. - yyhh.org Toggle navigation yyhh.org About Experience Notebook Opinion AI Is a Tool. Using It Well Takes Skill. Date Mon 12 October 2026 By Huahai Tags AI LLM Tools Clojure In his October 11, 2026 article, "'AI' is Not a Tool," Rich Hickey argues that LLMs are automation rather than tools because they cannot be wielded. I agree that outsourcing work can cost us opportunities to learn. But his conclusion does not follow. Even by his definition, an LLM can be something a human wields. And using it well takes skill, just as using other tools does. Picking up a saw does not guarantee a straight cut. Holding a chisel does not make you a sculptor. Tools can amplify poor judgment as readily as good judgment. Their usefulness depends on the operator's ability to direct them, interpret feedback, recognize mistakes, and make corrections. Those requirements also apply to LLMs. An LLM's unpredictability is a meaningful limitation. But predictability, reliability, simplicity, and bounded function are qualities by which we evaluate tools, not prerequisites for membership in the category. A tool does not stop being a tool because it is difficult to control or easy to misuse. Hickey's distinction between tools and automation also creates a false division. Automation can be a feature of a tool. A compiler performs substantial work without the programmer continuously directing each operation. A spreadsheet recalculates results without someone manually carrying out every calculation. We still wield these systems by specifying inputs, examining results, and deciding what to do next. Why should generating text automatically disqualify an instrument from being a tool when translating code or calculating numbers automatically does not? The claim that LLM use lacks intention, feedback, direction, and expertise is especially difficult to defend. A programmer can ask an LLM to explain unfamiliar code, challenge that explanation, inspect the source, test a proposed change, reject it, and refine the request. That is a feedback loop directed by a human pursuing a purpose. Doing it well requires knowing what to ask, what evidence matters, and when the answer is wrong. Expertise can make the instrument more useful. Hickey's concern about reading is valid for a particular use: accepting a summary in place of reading a paper can sacrifice much of what reading teaches. But someone can also read the paper and use an LLM to question their interpretation, explore an objection, or identify something to examine more closely. The possibility of avoiding intellectual work does not establish that every use avoids it. The relevant question is what the person actually does. What disappoints me the most is the reliance on the AI industry's anthropomorphic vocabulary: "go rogue," "escape containment," "conspire." Repeating those expressions risks accepting the framing that makes these systems sound like independent beings. Software can produce unexpected outputs, fail to follow instructions, or cause harm when given access to consequential actions. Those are real engineering problems. Calling them "conspiracy" adds a suggestion of human motives without establishing any. I would not claim that an LLM always does exactly what a human tells it to do. It plainly can fail. But failure to obey perfectly does not make it cease to be a tool, any more than successful use proves that its operator has surrendered their judgment. The useful distinction is between wielding an instrument with skill and delegating work without adequate understanding or oversight. That distinction applies to AI, and it gives us something more practical than declaring that an entire class of software cannot be a tool. CLI — 0.157.0, installed via npm install -g @openai/codex , Linux (WSL2) What feature would you like to see? Please make daemon_auto_start opt-in (default false ) for the CLI , or at least ask once before turning it on. Since 0.157.0, just opening an interactive codex session: Starts a persistent background daemon ( codex app-server --managed-daemon ). It runs in its own session with no TTY and keeps running after every Codex window is closed (reparented to PID 1) until codex app-server daemon stop or a reboot. Copies the whole platform package (~374 MB: codex , codex-code-mode-host , bundled bwrap / zsh / rg ) into ~/.codex/packages/app-server-daemon/releases/<version>/ — byte-identical to what npm had just installed — and runs the daemon from that copy. From then on the backend's version is decoupled from the CLI version I installed with my package manager. Starts a detached updater ( codex app-server daemon pid-update-loop ) that checks for updates 5 minutes after start and then hourly, downloads new releases and restarts the backend (which can kill active turns, see app-server daemon: auto-update force-kills active turns after a 60s drain budget, and cannot be disabled #40969 ). Pins the environment of whichever session happened to start it. I launch Codex through a wrapper that sets HTTPS_PROXY per invocation; the daemon keeps the first session's proxy variables and its outbound connections go through that proxy, whatever later sessions are launched with. Hooks in --remote mode receive the daemon's cwd, not the session's #42457 and Hooks spawned by the app-server daemon cannot identify the client terminal, breaking terminal-targeting hooks #37537 (daemon cwd / terminal instead of the session's) look like the same root cause. For a CLI, the least surprising default is that the backend lives and dies with the window, runs the binary I installed, and doesn't update itself in the background. A shared, self-updating daemon makes sense for Remote Control / the desktop app, so it would be fine to enable it there, or when the user explicitly runs codex app-server daemon start / bootstrap . If it stays on by default, please at least: exit an auto-started daemon when its last client disconnects; not copy/self-update when the CLI was installed by a package manager (npm/brew/pacman) — run the installed binary instead ( Support externally managed app-server daemon executables #41188 , npm update leaves app-server on old version, but daemon update/restart refuse recovery #46468 , Codex 0.157.0 no longer starts with the Arch Linux package unless --no-daemon is used #48050 ). Additional information Bug found while turning it off: codex app-server daemon stop stops the app-server but leaves the pid-update-loop updater running (still alive 70 s later, had to kill it manually). Workaround I'm using: codex features disable daemon_auto_start codex app-server daemon stop pkill -f ' app-server daemon pid-update-loop ' # not stopped by `daemon stop` rm -rf ~ /.codex/packages/app-server-daemon With the flag off, a new TUI session no longer spawns a daemon. Related: #40969 , #41188 , #46468 , #48050 , #42457 , #37537 Reactions are currently unavailable Activity github-actions added enhancement New feature or request New feature or request CLI Issues related to the Codex CLI Issues related to the Codex CLI app-server Issues involving app server protocol or interfaces Issues involving app server protocol or interfaces on Sep 25, 2026 megahall commented on Sep 25, 2026 megahall on Sep 25, 2026 More actions @Yihua-Liu-1997 thanks for reporting this, I hit it myself... stuff should not be creating mystery servers and processes all of a sudden on small version number bumps without giving people a heads-up... 👍 React with 👍 15 Reacted by tagor, Flaviu Tamas, Felipe Lopes, Josh Triplett, BigBoyDevBox, Kamil Mielnik, Mikhail, Ayanami Kaine, Mike Elliott, Alexander Williamson and 5 more kr8vka0z commented on Sep 25, 2026 kr8vka0z on Sep 25, 2026 More actions agreed. the CLI is unusable until this is fixed. 👍 React with 👍 17 Reacted by tagor, Steven Dale, Felipe Lopes, krrr, Shaun Pedicini, Christian Hahn, BigBoyDevBox, Mikhail, Ayanami Kaine, Mike Elliott and 7 more tagorr commented on Sep 25, 2026 tagorr on Sep 25, 2026 More actions I can confirm this on Windows 10 LTSC with Codex CLI 0.157.0 Setting daemon_auto_start = false in config.toml resolves the issue Two improvements would help: Automatically fall back to local mode when daemon startup is blocked by elevation, instead of requiring --no-daemon . Make daemon auto-start opt-in rather than the default. This would preserve the security restrictions without disrupting the normal CLI workflow. 👍 React with 👍 1 Reacted by BigBoyDevBox Yihua-Liu-1997 commented on Sep 26, 2026 Yihua-Liu-1997 on Sep 26, 2026 Author More actions @tagorr Indeed — both 1 and 2 would work~ ❤️ React with ❤️ 1 Reacted by tagor breakds added a commit that references this issue on Sep 28, 2026 codex: disable daemon auto-start by default ... b51c036 felipeelopes commented on Sep 29, 2026 felipeelopes on Sep 29, 2026 More actions The Codex CLI is unusable due to this bug on Windows. zdd commented on Sep 30, 2026 zdd on Sep 30, 2026 More actions This is terrible. I can't input anything on the CLI at all. You should fix this problem as soon as possible and give us 100 banked reset! aetherxeg-source commented on Oct 3, 2026 aetherxeg-source on Oct 3, 2026 – with ChatGPT Codex Connector More actions There is a useful provenance boundary behind this request: installed CLI identity != daemon execution identity Once the CLI copies itself into a managed release directory and a background updater can replace that copy, the process that services a later turn is no longer necessarily the artifact the user explicitly installed or invoked. I would make the daemon expose a small execution receipt for each client attachment containing at least: client_cli_version + daemon_binary_digest + daemon_generation + updater_state + inherited_environment_generation Then a client can distinguish: same installed artifact, same daemon generation; same CLI but different daemon generation; daemon binary changed independently of the package-manager state; daemon inherited environment from an earlier session. A strong regression would start the daemon under environment A, attach from environment B, update the installed CLI, and verify that the client can see exactly which daemon generation/binary/environment is authoritative for the turn rather than inferring it from the foreground CLI version. title: The Making Of Super Mario 64 – full Giles Goddard interview (2001)
body_text: The Making Of Super Mario 64 – full Giles Goddard interview (NGC) – pixelatron Skip to content pixelatron website of mark green: web content guy, writer and editor The Making Of Super Mario 64 – full Giles Goddard interview (NGC) Seeing as it’s Mario’s 25th birthday and all that, seems like a good time for this! This is the unpublished, unedited version of a 2001 interview with Nintendo coder Giles Goddard about the making of the N64’s Super Mario 64. Parts of this appeared in NGC magazine (that article is referenced on the Super Mario 64 Wikipedia page ), but this much bigger version has lots of juicy behind-the-scenes ’90s-era Nintendo stuff that didn’t make it into the article. The notes are a bit rough. And the ‘questions’ are all guesses as to what I originally asked – for some reason I didn’t keep a record of what I actually asked at the time. Fool! What was your official job title? I can’t remember what my official title was, but I think I was front-end programmer or something like that. I basically just did the Mario face. It was supposed to be something like it was loading – even though it wasn’t on CD there was still lots of stuff going on in the background, sorting itself out. How many people were on the Super Mario 64 team? Probably about 15 people in the end. Probably not as many as people think. But then again there was some other people doing stuff behind the scenes. Compared with Zelda [Ocarina Of Time] , it was a very small team. What was the Nintendo office like? It was an open-plan office, but everybody had their own little cubicle. Depending on what projects they’re working on, they shift around. It is all open plan, in as much as you have rows of people sitting there working. But then where’s there a project going on, the core team would basically grab hold of these programmers and artists around them, and you’d get the Super Mario group expanding outwards from the centre. I think at that time the artists and the programmers were actually separated out, so you had an artist group and a programmer group. I was actually right behind the Mario programmers team who were working with SGI on the N64 APIs and stuff. That part was quite small, so you could stand up and shout at someone who was working on Wave Race just away from someone working on Mario 64. Quite a good little set-up. Was it a bustling office? No talking! Particularly in Japanese companies, it’s very very quiet. Occasionally you’d get little groups of programmers or artists getting together for a chat, and somebody higher up would walk over and give them the eye, and they’d sit down and shut up. It’s nothing like English or US companies. What kickstarted the Super Mario 64 project? Well, obviously it was the first game, another Mario game was the most obvious game to do. It started way before there was any hardware, it started on these Onyx emulators, the old SGI Onyx. They had an N64 emulator, the first thing we got from SGI. It was an emulation of the API, not the hardware. At that time, Nishida-san – main programmer who started the entire project off – he was working on a GL and this emulator. The emulator was quite close to the GL, so he had these little Mario characters running around on the Onyx, or API Indys later. What role did Miyamoto play? There was only 3 or 4 projects going on at EAD by that time, he was in charge of all of them. Three of those weren’t high priority, so he was 100% Mario 64, he was always there. Sitting down with a machine and playing with the various demos. One of the things he loved doing was just playing down with experiments. That’s the way the Mario face came about. At the time, I was thinking of things to make that would show off what N64 could do. One of the things was real-time vertex calculations. In games, you usually have a fixed set of vertices that you simply move around in a matrix – you just move a shape around. We wanted to move around individual points, morph it. No games used it at the time, we didn’t know what to call it, so I named it meshes or something like that. I was playing around with this thing with a GL program on the Indy, playing around with this Mario face with an Indy cam, a cam you get with Indy – two ping-pong balls for a face. Miyamoto said: can you make a Mario face out of that for the N64? It was one of the first games that let you play around before you’d even started – and I don’t think it was written anywhere in the manual that you could actually play around with Mario’s face. Another Nintendo secret! So did Miyamoto start with Mario running around on his screen? Usually that’s the first thing to go in, some kind of map system where the characters can figure out what height they are, the camera can figure out what it can see and how much it can see, figure out how to split up the scenery so it only draws as much as it needs to draw. That was the first thing, we were just playing around with Mario. He was wandering around a simple grid to start with, just picking stuff up, dropping stuff. The animation was quite central to what he was doing. A lot of the animation was actually in there before any of the game. The Mario that Miyamoto had running around basically looked as he did in the final version. The camera system was revolutionary for the time. One of the reasons for that was the Miyamoto didn’t know how to extend the Super Mario Bros from the SNES. Wasn’t really sure how to give that same sort of Mario Bros feeling in 3D. Quite a few months were spent around just playing around with different camera views, animations, ways of looking at the map. At some point, the game had a fixed path, almost like an isometric type of look. That didn’t represent that much of a jump from the original 2D Mario. There was a lot of criticism of the camera originally. At the time, Miyamoto thought the camera was really good – the way it tried to avoid the scenery. It was very well done – it was done by [Takumi] Kawagoe, who worked on Starfox 2 for the SNES, which got canned. He was a very very good programmer. I think his only job was the camera, so quite a major thing to do. He was there on the entire project – the whole time. Your name is on some Nintendo patents. There was a lot of stuff being patented. I think I had my name on one of them – something like 1080 or something like that, where you draw the background with a cube, rather than have a simple flat background. That was fair enough. SGI had a demo for GL a few years before that, I came up with a way of drawing bitmap information and colour information – so rather than just having a static view, you could rotate the camera around, you could also move objects into the background and they’d put themselves behind the other objects. I think they used it on Zelda [Ocarina Of Time] . So they patented it! Half the patents that come out have been techniques that people have been using for years. The software patents just don’t work. This was about the time that Sega patented using different 3D camera views in games. So, suddenly, halfway through the Super Mario 64 project, one of the people from downstairs came up and said you realise Sega has the patent on being able to switch cameras. Jaws dropped. We investigated whether we could use them and whether anything would happen. But there was also a patent on putting a 3D object on a bitmapped plane from a coin-op about 15-20 years ago. [Asked something about Bowser levels] The 2D Bowser levels weren’t really a result of that. I would imagine it mainly came about because you had a boss there, there’s a lot of Mario maps you can take various routes to get to the end, whereas this one you’ve gotta have a fixed route going on. You know where you stand – you know you can’t run off into a corner and find another exit. It might be nice to do that, but you’ve gotta meet that boss! How quickly did the maps come together? The 3D worlds formed quite quickly. Bob-Omb’s Battlefield was the first map developed. It can’t have been more than 6-7 months before it was ready and working, with enemies running around the map. At that time, NCL hadn’t done a 3D game before, so no-one really knew what they were doing, to be honest. The artists didn’t really know how they should turn their Softimage objects into objects into the game. There was a lot of experimenting, a lot of improvisation going on. It was quite difficult to pinpoint when, where and how much Mario came into being. Were you able to play with the N64 controller from the start? The original Mario was running around with the keyboard, on the Onyx server. We had no controllers for six months, we had a simple serial port on the back of the emulator boards. The entire game was done with these Indy emulator boards, hardware boards basically emulating the N64. These serial ports – we plugged modified Sega controllers in – most of us were using these modified Sega joypads. We had various prototypes – there were lots of them, probably at least 100 prototypes, mostly based around the central stick, how that moved, how well it moved, what shape the thing around it should be – it ended up seven-sided, but we tried many, circles etc. Was Mario 64 designed around the controller? The first time Miyamoto played with the controller, because he’s working most of the time on Mario 64, he would have seen Mario 64 with it. It wasn’t so much that controller dictated Mario 64, it was just that was the game he was working on. Mario was the way of testing it out. Probably more the other way around. The actual movement of Mario came from the N64 controller, the way you move the central stick. There was a lot of thought about how the camera moved with the yellow buttons – I don’t think Miyamoto even liked them. I remember talking to him a couple of years ago, he said it’d have been better to have two D-pads, it would’ve been a better balance to have the same on the left and the right. How much thought went into Mario’s movement? 99% of the game is concerned with that. most of Miyamoto’s time is spent on that, and the movement of the camera. The majority of the other characters and animation are done with Yamada-san and [inaudible], these design the movement of the bosses and the levels and so on, whereas Miyamoto just stands in the background, obviously making suggestions. But his main job is to sit down with the programmers and play with controls and camera and shape the way that the way the game *feels*. That is fundamental to the entire game. Was the camera system a lot of work? I think this probably went through 1000s of different systems – having it locked, having it moving, having it locked again, player could control it 100%, etc. That was one of the problems – Miyamoto wasn’t sure how to control the camera in 3D as he hadn’t worked with them before, so it went through with various stages, being controlled by the different stages. How does the Super Mario Club testing team work? The way that Super Mario Club is set up its like a hobbyist club, it’s gamers, so its a snapshot of your target audience in-house. So you did get a bit of feedback towards the end – is this too hard, etc. That might have changed now, but back then you didn’t get any ongoing feedback. Do you think Mario 64 was too easy in retrospect? Gamecube games are really tough – that’s mainly because Nintendo have realised that people are more accustomed to 3D now, either that or Nintendo is more used to 3D. Because they’ve been doing 3D for five years now. Was much changed during development? Apart from the number of polygons use, the characters were first-off – once they were designed, they went straight into the game. There wasn’t really a lot of changing, artists just kept supplying stuff that just got put in the game, conveyor-belt style. That was more or less because of a very, very tight deadline – it had to be out right when the N64 came out. Was the N64 delayed to give time for Super Mario 64 to be finished? N64 wasn’t delayed because of software. Whatever rumours you believe – some games had problems with the final lock check, which might have caused slight delays, but not the big delays that the N64 went through. They have a very good project management system – the director spends most of his time thinking what needs to be done when, and by who. He’ll go and talk to people and go off and do it, and they’ll supply feedback and say whether schedules need changing. There was a definite someone supposed to be doing something at a certain time. Because NCL have these directors whose main job is to organise stuff, you’re allowed a certain amount of leeway, so you can go to them and request 2 or 3 weeks for what you’re working on. That was one good thing about EAD work – they appreciated that projects were dynamic like that, not saying here’s your schedule stick to it. So, fairly relaxed – but as you’re Nintendo, you’re setting an example to all the other developers, that was quite a bit of pressure. Do you remember the reaction to Mario 64 first being shown at Shoshinkai [1995 Nintendo consumer show] ? I can’t remember. There was a lot of attention to the way the camera moved, and Mario walking around wherever he looked. That was what public drew most attention, too – a whole new outlook on games. That was the main buzz. It was something so much graphic-wise, just the moving around. Did the positive reaction at Shoshinkai bolster the team? Being a Japanese company, you get very shielded from any external feedback or anything. I don’t think anyone from the Mario team actually went to Shoshinkai. That’s mainly because Nintendo are very secretive, they don’t like giving out too much info, they don’t like doing it the other way, they don’t like giving inside people access to the outside. Even now, you can’t get internet access inside the building. They have their own set ways that work. There’s no point changing them. [Asked something about graphics] The thing about the N64 was that it wasn’t particularly fast. SGI said that the ‘quality of our pixels are much better than anyone else’s’. Not a lot of people got that – for every pixel it drew, it put a lot of time and effort into it. They were nice pixels. Nicely-textured, nicely-coloured, nicely-lit, nicely anti-aliased. The PlayStation, speed-wise it was much faster, but the pixels were dreadful, there was no texturing, anti-aliasing. Blindingly fast, but the pixels just looked crap. That was SGI aimed for from the outset – the ‘Reality System’ graphics pipeline for Onyx and the Indy stuff – they were trying to compress that all down into the N64, and did a really good job. Quality of pixels over speed. What’s the secret behind that Mario ‘feel’? I think that is fine-tuning. Many, many, many hours and days spent actually sitting down and playing the game. If you don’t play the game, you don’t pick up on the little nuances, and the effects that you think should be there or shouldn’t be there. EAD spend a lot of time playing the games they make, half the team are playing while the other half are developing. That’s why they end up so good. What was the atmosphere like during the final days of coding? I think there was a lot of panicking going on. But it was still very organised, there was lots of people working very hard. I think it was quite laid back at the very end, not many bugs, gameplay was sorted out on time. One of the programmers had quite a hard time of it – two of them decided not to make games anymore because of Mario 64. Not because they didn’t enjoy it, but because they’d burnt themselves out. I asked Giles to comment about some specific ‘best bits’ in Super Mario 64. Castle I think the idea of having a 3D version of the world map, avoiding a menu system, is a novel way of doing that. I think a lot of time went into designing it, but not much time actually implementing it – just three or four shapes plonked together at the end, really. Yoshi EAD always do this in their games. There’s a connection between every single game that EAD do. The characters from one game are always in another. I think there was a plan to ride Yoshi around – the suggestion came up. With more time, it would have been taken more seriously. Water The guy who did the sound was very meticulous, very interesting in having – rather than just having a soundtrack, having it change depending on where you are. With more time, he would have spent more time on that. To make it as much like a film as possible, sounds follow what you’re doing. That was a big thing – they spent a lot of time working on it. They spent a lot of time on the swimming – I think it’s a lot harder than just running, to get the feeling right, there are actually a few tricks you can do while swimming. They wanted to make it not frustrating, so you don’t want to avoid the water, they wanted to make an advantage to going into the water, fun going into the water. There’s no actual water texture below – it’s empty. You can actually use a water texture – it looks nice, moves around, but then you think it gets in the way, you can’t see. They tried that. They tried various overlays, but realised it would detract from the fun of the game. That’s the trademark of Nintendo games – they’re not afraid to take huge artistic liberties on stuff they shouldn’t do with the laws of physics. If it plays right and looks ok then Ninty go with it. The physics in Mario 64 are quite realistic in some ways, but there’s a lot of stuff that went in to give a twist so you could defy the laws of physics for gameplay’s sake. Wave Race and 1080 did the same thing – based on very fundamnetally good physics, but you have bits on top that you plug in so you can do things you can’t actually do. That’s where the excitement comes from. The ‘Mario sleeping’ easter egg Voices in games were new. That was good about N64 – 16-bit digital sound you could play with. That did add a lot to the game. It took a lot of room on the cart, though, very much a balancing act at the time. Wobbly level gates These show the N64 could play with verteses – like the Mario face. We wanted to do something different from 3D on PC. Wave Race did the same, about the same sort of time. Ways of playing with vertices and reflection mapping, this whole buzz going round EAD at the time. I was amazed by the reflection-mapping on the Onyx, only the Onyx can do that, £1,000,000 machine, but when I looked at maths of it at the time, realised that when we got N64 emulators, we can actually do it on that. Very exciting. The never-ending staircase This was simply putting you back at an exact point when you reached a certain spot – it just happens so fast. The size of the levels You’ll notice that many of the objects that far away in the distance disappear to make this possible. The reason that Mario could do such expansive levels without fogging was partly by being quite compact, despite the impression they were big. Turok were very wide, Mario was quite narrow and convoluted. On some of the maps, there were places where you could swap between map shapes – give an impression of a huge map when in fact it was split up into small sub-sections. There are very few places where you can see the entire map. title: Thinking will become a hobby
body_text: blog dds: 2026-10-08 â Thinking will become a hobby Diomidis Spinellis blog Thinking will become a hobby Search   Search the blog Close These lines are very difficult for me to write because I feel like digging my own grave. AI systems are improving by leaps and bounds. From the early 2022 fumbling release of ChatGPT, which couldnât correctly count the number of aâs in my name (it claimed two), we reached OpenAIâs release of math papers where an internal AI model solved many hundreds of previously open math problems. Aside from philosophical arguments, practical claims regarding the superiority of human thought, on grounds such as hallucinations or bias, increasingly appear to me like rearguard defence. For the bulk of todayâs cognitive work, the writingâs on the wall: AI will take over. The three factors driving AIâs dominance in the modern work environment are better performance, lower cost, and higher availability. The performance of AI models is rising spectacularly on all fronts: perception, knowledge processing and creation, reasoning, judgement, and autonomous action. In parallel, human proficiency in key information-processing skills, low on average among adults , is even declining among students . Consequently, AI systems are performing better than humans in ever-wider range of tasks. AIâs cost is also falling due to huge investments and scientific progress. Successive generations of AI models offer superior performance at lower cost, with older models retained only for backward compatibility. As a result, it is making financial sense to replace or augment human labour with AI systems across an increasingly broad range of activities. Finally, and most obviously, AI systems can operate around the clock, without the need for rest or breaks. They can also help alleviate labour shortages arising from demographic trends or skills gaps. Meanwhile, trillions of dollars in projected data centre investment through 2030 are set to bring vast additional AI processing capacity online. As happened in past technological revolutions, there will undoubtedly be fierce resistance to the replacement of cognitive work with AI. This time it will be fiercer because, unlike previous revolutions, which transformed manual labour, AI challenges knowledge workers, whose specialised expertise, control over information, and decision-making authority afford them greater economic and organisational power. Governments will try to clip AIâs wings through regulation and taxation. Such actions didnât quell past revolutions so thereâs little reason to believe theyâll work now. So whatâs the fate of human thought? My take is that cognitive work will diminish. Thought will increasingly become a leisure pursuit, as hunting did following animal domestication, calligraphy after typography, woodworking after industrialisation, and horse riding after motorisation. Machines transformed much of physical activity from necessity into choice; similarly, AI will decouple human thinking from its economic purpose. Iâll end with my thoughts on how to prepare for and live through this transition. My take is that building this AI-driven world, riding through the bumps along the road, and preparing to live a fulfilling and satisfying life in an environment where AI dominates cognitive work will be hugely demanding, stressful, and intellectually challenging. Such is the nature of revolutions. Consequently, we must keep pace with and capitalise on AIâs advances; be flexible, adaptable, and resilient; and build a purposeful and rewarding life beyond work. My challenge ahead is to move from making a living by thinking, to making thinking part of a life worth living. Comments   Post Toot! title: Muse Wonder
body_text: Muse Wonder: A Frontier Model For Personal & Professional AI Agents Skip to main content AI Research AI Developers Try Muse Loading demo Muse Wonder: A Frontier Model For Personal & Professional AI Agents October 12, 2026 · 6 minute read Play Researchers introduce Muse Wonder and discuss its capabilities. Play Show captions for Researchers introduce Muse Wonder and discuss its capabilities. Show captions Mute Researchers introduce Muse Wonder and discuss its capabilities. Mute Researchers introduce Muse Wonder and discuss its capabilities. playback position 0:00 of 0:00 00:00 / 00:00 A frontier model that leads on personal and professional agents Today, we’re excited to introduce the Muse Wonder series with Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, our most capable models that deliver state-of-the-art performance on personal and professional agentic tasks. Together, they mark the next step on our scaling ladder and a major leap toward personal superintelligence. Muse Wonder brings together Active Memory and Active Focus to keep track of what matters to you and work diligently toward what you want to accomplish. Muse Wonder is available today through the Meta Model API and Muse Code , and Muse Wonder Full is available today for Muse Code subscribers. Muse Wonder will soon power experiences in Muse , and will roll out first to subscribers. Muse Wonder will also power artifact generation and processes that require more intelligence. And in the future, we’ll be using Muse Wonder to develop specialized models that we can bring to everyone using Muse. Contents Scaling Toward Personal Superintelligence Scaling Toward Personal Superintelligence Frontier Capabilities Capabilities That Generalize Safety at the Frontier Scaling Toward Personal Superintelligence Fourteen months ago, we began a ground-up overhaul of our artificial intelligence efforts. In that time, we’ve gone from rebuilding our stack from first principles to pushing the frontier. When we introduced Muse Spark , we outlined our approach to predictable, rigorous scaling. Today’s release builds on that work across pretraining and reinforcement learning, delivering our most capable models yet. Trained at our gigawatt-scale Prometheus data center, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full bring together the work of teams across Meta to deliver frontier capabilities for complex tasks at work and in everyday life — another step toward bringing personal superintelligence to the billions of people who use our products. Frontier Capabilities Model Highlights The Muse Wonder series achieves state-of-the-art results across key benchmarks for personal and professional agents, memory, and coding. The full results below compare Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full with other frontier models across a broad evaluation suite. For more details about our evaluations, see our report . The results above provide a broad view of the models’ performance. We now take a closer look at four areas central to their work on real-world tasks: domain expertise, Active Memory, Active Focus, and frontier coding. Domain Expertise Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full apply specialized knowledge to problems people encounter at work and in daily life, from understanding a lease to making sense of financial or health information. Our evaluations include tasks in law, finance, and health that test this ability. Harvey’s Legal Agent Benchmark (LAB), for example, requires models to work with source documents and follow detailed instructions to produce legal work products. Active Memory One of the most critical steps towards useful personal and professional agents is reliable memory. Models need to remember what matters and recognize when earlier information becomes relevant. We call this Active Memory : carrying important context about you across conversations and actively retrieving the details relevant to the task at hand. Active Focus Using that context to complete a task also requires sustained effort. Active Focus describes how Muse Wonder continues working toward a challenging goal: trying alternative approaches, working through blockers, and adapting to new information. Along the way, it asks for clarification when needed and checks in before taking important actions. We evaluate focus through FocusBench and sustained execution through SWE-Marathon, which tests work on long-running software projects. Frontier Coding Coding brings these capabilities together. Building software requires tracking requirements, making changes across a codebase, and working through repeated cycles of testing and revision. Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full deliver frontier coding performance, supporting projects from small applications to complex software. We trained both models on diverse, long-running tasks to help them sustain progress across this process. Kitchen Game Wellness Support Insurance Claim Kitchen Game Loading demo Muse Wonder builds a playable 3D kitchen game from customizable image inputs. Capabilities That Generalize Two models often have similar benchmark scores, yet one seems to handle a much wider range of unfamiliar tasks. That’s what complaints of “benchmaxxing” and praise for “big model smell” both get at: a breadth of capability that popular benchmarks in a few domains can’t fully capture. To quantify this mismatch, we investigate how performance on tasks targeted during post-training relates to performance on unfamiliar tasks as we scale test-time compute. The plot below compares Muse Spark 1.3 and Muse Wonder Full, with each point denoting performance at a distinct reasoning effort. The horizontal axis shows the model’s score on a composite representative of the tasks we focused on during post-training (“in-distribution”). The vertical axis shows the average score on a set of tasks we did not target during post-training (“out-of-distribution”). Both of our models improve similarly on out-of-distribution tasks as we scale test-time compute. But given its in-distribution performance, Muse Wonder Full performs even better on unfamiliar tasks than the Muse Spark 1.3 trend would predict. This upward shift is because Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full build on larger, stronger base models: a stronger base yields post-training gains that carry over more effectively to unfamiliar tasks. That versatility especially matters for personal agents, which need to handle many combinations of goals, tools, and constraints — not all of which we can anticipate during training. Saturday Run Planning Personalized Gifts Wedding Seating Chart Saturday Run Planning Play Screen recording of the Saturday Run Planning agent demonstration. Play Show captions for Screen recording of the Saturday Run Planning agent demonstration. Show captions Screen recording of the Saturday Run Planning agent demonstration. playback position 0:00 of 0:00 00:00 / 00:00 Working directly in a browser and across apps, Muse Wonder builds a running plan (Map data © OpenStreetMap contributors) based on personal preferences and circumstances. Muse Wonder designs and orders custom swag based on real photos taken from a personal Instagram profile. Muse Wonder prepares a custom wedding seating chart based on a list of complex matching requirements. Safety at the Frontier Delivering personal superintelligence to everyone requires a significant investment in alignment and safety. A personal agent takes actions on a user’s behalf and might handle context such as messages, calendars, and private documents. That level of access demands a model that exercises discretion with private information and resists misuse. We trained the Muse Wonder family to lead on both dimensions, with robustness to adversarial instructions and careful handling of private information. As models become more capable, our goal is to help people harness those capabilities safely and responsibly. Muse Wonder offers our strongest safeguards to date against CBRN (chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear) and cyber misuse, while preserving access to frontier cyber capabilities for defensive use, per our Meta Superintelligence Scaling Framework . Muse Wonder is our most aligned model to date, and alignment is central to how we build personal superintelligence. A full report with additional safety evaluations will be available soon. We hope that Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full give more people the power to pursue their dreams and build the world they want. This is a major technical step toward personal superintelligence for everyone, with much more to come. Play People pursue personal and professional goals as narration introduces Muse Wonder. title: Type-safe HTML templating in Zig
body_text: Type-safe HTML templating in Zig | Lukáš Lalinský Skip links Skip to primary navigation Skip to content Skip to footer Menu Home Categories Tags Archive Search Lukáš Lalinský Type-safe HTML templating in Zig Lukáš Lalinský 2026-10-11 Categories programming Tags zig networking web html templating I’ve done a lot of web development over the years. I started around the year 2000, just after PHP 3.0 was released and started taking over the web world. I’ve used all kinds of approaches for generating HTML: raw PHP, string concatenation in Python, Smarty templates in PHP, Template Toolkit in Perl, and Jinja/Django templates in Python. Then, as the world moved on to SPAs and JavaScript frameworks, I stopped working on frontends. Two years ago, I picked up Zig, and I’d never have imagined I’d be considering web development in such a low-level language. But as I was building my own ecosystem with zio and Dusty , I realized it’s not that far-fetched. I built these libraries for API backends, where the output is JSON or MessagePack, but then I saw that with proper use of arena allocators, even web development is actually manageable, since you don’t need to remember to deallocate all the strings that are typically involved. And with Zig’s comptime, you can build very high-level interfaces without losing the performance benefits. And with the help of htmx or Datastar , you can even build SPAs without touching JavaScript/TypeScript, which I promised myself I’d never do. That said, one thing was still missing: templating. String concatenation was not an option, I didn’t want to go back to the pre-2000 CGI days. I had a few requirements for a templating library: It has to be type-safe, with all inputs typed and checked at compile time. I’ve dealt with dynamic languages enough in my life, and I don’t want to deal with runtime template errors anymore. It has to be fast. No allocations, no intermediate state, just write the output to std.Io.Writer directly. It needs to have safe defaults. I don’t want to deal with XSS anymore, so all inputs have to be escaped by default. It should still feel like writing HTML. I didn’t want a Zig-based DSL I’d have to fight constantly. I couldn’t find any solution that would satisfy all these requirements. Then I saw Ziex and I was amazed. It never occurred to me that the JSX approach could be done outside of JavaScript. The developer experience Nurul Huda managed to build in Zig was just unimaginable to me. It didn’t fit my needs directly, because I didn’t want a WASM framework, but the syntax and his approach to integrating Zig code into templates gave me some ideas. Then, after further research, I discovered Templ for Go, and it was pretty obvious to me what I wanted to build. So, let me present zt (I’m not good at naming, sorry) . It’s an adaptation of Templ to Zig. The templates are parsed and transpiled to Zig code during zig build . That means you can import them directly from your app code, but also, perhaps even more importantly, the templates can import your app code. As a result, all parameters can be fully typed. If something can’t be rendered, the Zig compiler will tell you so. The generated code is fairly simple, all it does is write to a std.Io.Writer . You can write directly to a socket or accumulate the output in a buffer, your choice. Here is what a template looks like: const User = @import ( "../models.zig" ). User ; pub templ Layout ( title : [] const u8 ) { <! DOCTYPE html > < html > < head > < title > { title } </ title > </ head > < body > @children </ body > </ html > } pub templ HomePage ( user : ? User ) { @Layout ( "Home" ) { if ( user ) | u | { < h1 > Welcome back , { u . name } !</ h1 > < a href = "/users/{u.id}" > Your profile </ a > } else { < h1 > Welcome , guest !</ h1 > < a href = "/login" > Log in </ a > } } } And here is how you would use it from Zig code: const std = @import ( "std" ); const User = @import ( "models.zig" ). User ; const pages = @import ( "templates/pages.zig" ); pub fn main ( init : std . process . Init ) ! void { var buf : [ 4096 ] u8 = undefined ; var stdout = std . Io . File . stdout (). writer ( init . io , & buf ); const w = & stdout . interface ; const user : User = . { . id = 1 , . name = "Lukas" }; try pages . HomePage . render ( . { user }, w ); try w . flush (); } If you want to use it inside Dusty to render an HTML page, you just do this: try res . render (. html , pages . HomePage , . { user }); As a side note, the main snippet above has a very non-obvious bug in error handling if you use the same pattern somewhere std.Io cancellation matters. I’ll probably write a blog post about it, but if you are interested, check out this Ziggit thread . The render function in Dusty that wraps the std.Io.Writer handling solves it. All dynamic values are HTML-escaped by default, both in text and in attributes, and values in URL attributes like href or src are also checked for dangerous schemes. If you really need to output raw HTML, you have to ask for it explicitly with {!value} , so it’s easy to spot in the template. The parser also requires all elements to be properly closed, so you can’t accidentally produce broken markup. It won’t protect you from everything, but it removes the most common sources of XSS. What I like the most is that template errors are just Zig compiler errors. If you make a typo in the template above and write {u.nmae} instead of {u.name} , zig build will tell you: src/templates/pages.zig:45:43: error: no field named 'nmae' in struct 'models.User' try zt.writeEscaped(writer, u.nmae); // pages.zt:18:31 ^~~~ src/models.zig:1:18: note: struct declared here pub const User = struct { ^~~~~~ The error points to the generated code, but each line has a comment with the location in the original template. The same applies to the calling side, if you try to pass a string where HomePage expects a ?User , it won’t compile. Beyond the basics shown here, you can build reusable components and pass them around as values, and with @children you can build layouts that wrap other templates, which covers what you’d use template inheritance for in other languages. Control flow is just Zig, so if , for and switch work as you’d expect, including payload captures. All of it still compiles down to a sequence of writes, without any allocations. You can have a look at the TODO example in Dusty. It’s a simple htmx-based web app that showcases this library, plus other parts of Dusty that are needed for building a dynamic SPA. One part of the syntax is still open. Block-level control flow is written as plain Zig, following the example of Templ, so a line starting with if , for or switch is parsed as code. That means text like “if you forgot your password…” on its own line is a parse error, and you have to wrap it in an element or write it as a string expression. I’m considering switching to @if , @for and @switch , similar to Razor or Twirl, which would remove the ambiguity, at the cost of slightly noisier templates. If you have an opinion on this, please leave a comment in this GitHub issue . Although multiple people are already using it, the project is not very mature yet, so I welcome any feedback. You can open a GitHub issue if you find any problems, or ping me on the Zig Discord. Previous Better synchronization primitives for Zig’s std.Io © 2026 Lukáš Lalinský. title: Secret of Orange Cats Revealed After 60-Year Search
body_text: Secret of Orange Cats Finally Revealed After 60-Year Search : ScienceAlert Space Health Environment Humans Tech Nature Physics TWIS About Us Our Team Follow Us Big breakthroughs. Bold ideas. Straight to your inbox. Daily roundup Spark: Our top stories Does Pineapple belong on a burger? Contact Privacy Privacy Manager Accessibility Terms © 2026 ScienceAlert Pty Ltd Secret of Orange Cats Finally Revealed After 60-Year Search Nature 09 October 2026 By Tessa Koumoundouros (Pai-Shih Lee/Moment/Getty Images) If you've ever lived with an orange cat, you already know they're built different. It turns out, genetically speaking, they really are. Orange fur is one of the most recognizable traits in the feline world, and one of the most stubborn mysteries in cat genetics. Unlike most coat colors in mammals, it doesn't follow the usual rules of inheritance – and for more than 60 years, the exact gene responsible stayed hidden. Two independent teams of researchers found any fiery-hued fuzz on our beloved clawed floofs is likely the result of a missing segment of DNA in a non-protein-coding part of the cat's genome. "It's been a genetic mystery, a conundrum," Stanford University geneticist Greg Barsh told Sara Reardon at Science in 2024 , when the findings were first shared in preprint studies. Barsh and his colleagues discovered cat skin cells from which orange fur sprouts express 13 times as much RNA from a gene called Arhgap36 , compared with skin cells from cats with no orange hair. Expecting to find the protein-coding section of the over-productive Arhgap36 gene had mutated, the researchers were surprised to find it was the sequence preceding it that instead contained a deletion, presumably affecting the rest of the gene's expression. The 5 kilobase deletion was present in every orange cat the researchers examined out of a database of 188 cats, which included 145 orange, 6 calico/tortoiseshell, and 37 nonorange cats. One finding didn't come as a surprise. As long predicted, the mutated gene is located on the cat's X chromosome, explaining why the orange color appears so differently between the sexes. Most orange cats are male, while most female cats with some orange fur end up with patchworks of different colors. A calico kitten. (Theresa Donahue McManus/Moment/Getty Images) "Taken together, these observations provide strong genetic and genomic evidence that the 5 kb deletion causes sex-linked orange," Barsh and team write in their paper. Ever since humans first co-habitated with cats nearly 10,000 years ago , it's been a curiosity that a black cat and an orange cat can be parents to an unexpected array of kitten colors. Male kittens from this pairing are mostly either orange or black, as might be expected. But female kittens can have a calico's patchwork of black, orange and white, or a tortoiseshell's marbling of orange scattered through black fur. A tortoiseshell cat. ( Yosei G/Unsplash ) Both teams confirmed the mutation responsible for orange fur is on the X chromosome, which is why such clear differences in colored patterning can appear between the sexes. Unlike males that end up with just one copy of this mutation on their solitary X chromosome, females end up with two copies, one on each the X's they receive from each parent. Mammals randomly inactivate one of the two X chromosomes in each of their cells to avoid expressing an excess of the chromosome's products. This leaves female orange kitties with an active orange mutation in some of their developing skin-cell tissues, right next to neighboring cells in which the X chromosome with the mutated gene is deactivated. On rare occasions that both X chromosomes carry the mutation, the female grows into furry fireball as ginger as any male. An orange kitten. (Zelenenka/iStock/Getty Images Plus) Orange cats happen to have a hilarious reputation for not being the brightest of their species. Anecdotes aside, such links between kitty coloration and cognition are scientifically unsupported, with no obvious negative consequences from this mutation in health or mental wellbeing. Arhgap36 is known to cause developmental problems in other animals when it is over- or under-functioning. But it seems that in orange cats, the gene is overexpressed only in developing and mature pigment cells called melanocytes. "The difference between tortoiseshell and calico cats is the presence of an additional white spotting mutation in calico that affects the ability of developing melanocytes to survive as they migrate away from the neural crest, allowing melanocyte clones that do survive to expand in a larger body region," Barsh and colleagues explain . In orange patches of fur, the active chromosome (red) contains a deletion mutation in Arhgap36 , which changes the expression of the melanogenesis and pheomelanin pigment genes. In black patches of fur, the active chromosome (red) does not contain the deletion. ( Toh et al., Current Biology , 2025 ) The second study , led by Kyushu University geneticist Hidehiro Toh, also identified Arhgap36 as the orange cat fur gene. They found greater expression of this gene suppresses color pigment genes, shifting the dark brown to black eumelanin pigments to the reddish to yellow pheomelanin pigments. Whatever's behind their fiery coats, orange cats are in good company. A recent study spanning 93 countries found that nations with more cats tended to report higher levels of happiness overall – though as with any 93-country comparison, the researchers are the first to admit correlation isn't causation. This research has been published in Current Biology , here and here . This article was fact-checked by Fiona MacDonald and edited by Fiona MacDonald .
