title: 'AI' Is Not a Tool by Rich Hickey
body_text: 'AI' is Not a Tool Agree & Join LinkedIn By clicking Continue to join or sign in, you agree to LinkedIn’s User Agreement , Privacy Policy , and Cookie Policy . Sign in to view more content Create your free account or sign in to continue your search Email or phone Password Show Forgot password? Sign in Sign in with Email or New to LinkedIn? Join now By clicking Continue to join or sign in, you agree to LinkedIn’s User Agreement , Privacy Policy , and Cookie Policy . Skip to main content LinkedIn Top Content People Learning Jobs Games Join now Sign in 'AI' is Not a Tool Report this article Rich Hickey Rich Hickey Published Oct 12, 2026 + Follow (I keep delivering this as a quip, here's a bit more) First order of business - is ' tool ' going to have an interesting, distinguishing and thus illuminative meaning or be a mere platitudinous stand-in for "anything useful"? We'll save tool as "anyone/thing that can be exploited" for the AI titans, for whom VCs, politicians, wannabe-titan-CEOs, software devs, rural towns etc are all 'tools'. The pockets on the front of my shirts are useful (I need to keep my reading glasses handy), but they are not tools. Similarly, fast food drive-thru windows are useful, but are not tools (more later). Some definitions of ' tool ': a device or implement, especially one held in the hand, used to carry out a particular function an instrument (such as a hammer or saw) used or worked by hand : an instrument used by a handicraftsperson or laborer in their work What I like best - A tool is something you wield . wield - to use (as a tool or instrument) especially with full command or power : handle, manipulate, control Especially useful in that are: Held in your hand - a source of both control and feedback, and an indication of the intimacy of the act of use Power - force, energy transmission and direction, leverage etc Control - intention and continuous directing of the course of events Tools are implements with which you do something, they do not do things for you. Tool use builds, rewards, and often requires, expertise and skill. The continuous application of technique and energy, and sensory feedback, are essential to the buildup of expertise (from experiri - "try"). Good tools have many properties LLMs lack - they are predictable, reliable, deterministic, of bounded function, hopefully simple etc. What you learn while wielding a tool is something about the world, the task, the physics, logic etc of what you are trying to do or the situation you are trying to overcome. And often, something about yourself. As a lifelong tool builder and user, I know what tools are. LLMs are not tools. Control, sensory feedback, intention, intimacy, continuous direction, expertise etc are all missing from LLM use. LLMs are not wielded. LLMs are automation . automation - (of a device or process) working by itself with little or no direct human control. A drive-thru is not a tool for cooking, it is automation for avoiding cooking. LLMs are not tools with which you write code - they are automation with which you avoid writing code, to which you abdicate writing code. You don't direct the action of an LLM - you make requests and it acts on its own, without your energy or continuous direction. This request/automation cycle is not wielding, it's not control, it's not continuous, it's without feedback. What you are doing while using automation, instead of learning real-world truths, is attempting to divine the details du jour of some automaton. And striving to game them - e.g. ordering a custom burger (no onions) in order to get a freshly made one. Or filling voodoo.md with just the right incantations. You are only a software update from everything you've 'learned' being rendered obsolete by the latest algorithm. (A soggy cold burger from which the onions have been removed) You have traded working with the world to working for a capricious robot. It is a mistake to be haphazard about "tools" being equivalent to utility, e.g. saying - "the LLM didn't write my paper, I just used it as a tool to read and summarize some research papers". But you didn't wield it to read those papers (as you might a Kindle). It read the papers, not you. What do you miss by abdicating doing the reading? Pretty much everything. First and foremost, you miss learning how to write from those who can. You miss learning how to formulate an argument. You miss noticing things. You miss loading your background mind with fodder for novel ideas. You miss building trust in some authors and suspicion of others. You miss all the jokes. You miss all of the edges. You miss learning how to think. Tools don't get "misaligned", they don't "go rogue", they don't "escape containment", "conspire" etc. LLMs are not tools. I know many people use the phrase "just tools" simply to indicate "they are what you make of them". Except that's not true . Automation has intrinsic properties and differences from tools that you ignore at your peril. Rich Like Like Celebrate Support Love Insightful Funny Comment Copy LinkedIn Facebook X Share 551 61 Comments siavash mohammady 2m Report this comment Article is not ontologically clarifying anything. Argument could be used for any disruptive technology or tool like fire, money, steam engine, computer & ... Like Reply 1 Reaction Graham Perrin 1h Report this comment For clarity: I, the human, do something when I instruct AI, typically Claude, to do something. It's a tool. I asked Vibe: "Is it reasonable to describe AI as a tool?". https://chat.mistral.ai/work/eb5cc87d-8b94-43ec-9bcb-daef25ade478 tl;dr it's a reasonable and common description, but it's worth being precise about what it implies. Like Reply 1 Reaction Armando Baratti 3h Report this comment Nomenclature is a hard thing. Probably that's why it is so difficult to name variables and functions. We use words to mean things that the words can not explain completely. In this sense, independent of classifying LLMs, or agents or systems that we call incorrectly AI, as automation in opposition to tools, I think that the feeling of what Rich Hickey brings here is of great importance. The fact is that LLMs (I'll use the same name used in the article for simplicity) robs us from the control, from the experience of interacting and learning with the code we were producing by ourselves before. Many people have the sense that they can learn by reading how the automaton have solved the problem, but learn by seeing the job done is much poorer than learning by doing the work yourself. This hard part give us the chance to really fix the ideas on our minds and to prepare it to be able to explore new paths for new ideas or to build new mental tools to solve new kind of problems. When we take a shortcut we loose too much. All in the name of producing faster and faster (but we really need all this speed?). ... continues Like Reply 1 Reaction Vektor Memory 4h Report this comment Well then, it's a "magic tool" like a wizard. I'm OK with that... You can conjure up complex names and reclassify—but it is always a binary set of instructions/algorithms in a neural net. Until Neuralink joins millions into organic/binary cyborg chimeras. People in the past wouldn't understand how a human can control a drone with their brain, but it is going to happen via "Magic tools" Like Reply 1 Reaction Shaad Alaka 4h Report this comment Honestly, I think many of the tools that we can choose to use for things nowadays have a degree of automation about them. Tool or automation is not a binary classification, rather we have quite a few tools that automate certain things (as in, the automation is part of the tool, e.g. a calculator), while giving user control over certain other things. But so far, for most of our tools, the degree of automation/control had been fixed. With LLMs that is different now: you as a user are free to choose how much of the work you delegate. You can let the LLM generate a function, or you can let it generate the entire codebase. So you can choose yourself where it sits on that spectrum from tool to automation. Therefore I think it is wrong to say that LLMs are not a tool; that depends entirely on how the user is using the LLM, and in this sense they are in my opinion quite incomparable to anything else that had existed before. Some anecdotal evidence of this is the fact that there are people who are really "good" at using them and do not seem to suffer from atrophy in their skills and thinking, and then there are some other people who do experience these negative consequences from usage, of missing things as described in the article. AI coding agents generate more code, but not more software
body_text: AI coding agents generate more code, but not more software - Ars Technica Skip to content Ars Technica home Sections Forum Subscribe Search AI Biz & IT Cars Culture Gaming Health Policy Science Security Space Tech Feature Reviews AI Biz & IT Cars Culture Gaming Health Policy Science Security Space Tech Forum Subscribe Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only    Learn more Pin to story Theme HyperLight Day & Night Dark System Search Sign In Sign in dialog... Sign in Quantity, not quality AI coding agents generate more code, but not more software Study finds coding efficiency gains get “absorbed” by human review “bottleneck.” Kyle Orland – Oct 9, 2026 3:43 pm | 285 Here, let me just... yeah, can I lend you a hand here? Credit: Getty Images Here, let me just... yeah, can I lend you a hand here? Credit: Getty Images Text settings Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only    Learn more Minimize to nav Anyone who has even tangentially associated with computer programming knows that modern AI coding assistants and agents can be incredibly efficient at generating huge amounts of functional code . But coders making use of those tools also know better than to trust the accuracy of that code , meaning substantial effort needs to be spent reviewing any AI-generated output. A recent study of actual coding practices across hundreds of firms finds that human code review forms a significant “bottleneck” for the overall efficiency of AI coding tools, resulting in “little evidence that firms increase software output or reduce employment” by using them. Any efficiency increased during the actual coding phase, the study authors find, is “absorbed by downstream constraints in the production process”; as “the code review process significantly increases in length, pull requests are more likely to require revisions, and reviewers leave more comments.” Cut once, measure twice To come to these conclusions, Harvard University researchers Fiona Chen and James Stratton made use of aggregated analytics data from Jellyfish , which measures the granular output of engineering teams. That data encompasses 300 million individual “work events” (e.g., commits and pull requests) and issue management software data across more than 700,000 employees at over 700 relevant software development firms from 2021 through March of 2026. To assess the impact of AI tools on these firms, the researchers used a mix of directly measured AI usage and analyses of GitHub activity to determine when each company started introducing either AI coding assistants (which can help auto-complete code primarily authored by humans) and/or AI coding agents (which primarily write and submit code autonomously based on prompts) into their workflows. The researchers then perform some complicated math to determine a “difference of differences” regression on key variables both before and after the introduction of these tools at different points in time across different organizations. If there’s one thing AI coding agents are good at, it’s churning out a lot of code. Credit: Chen and Stratton If there’s one thing AI coding agents are good at, it’s churning out a lot of code. Credit: Chen and Stratton In terms of raw code being produced, the results are clear and stark. The introduction of AI coding agents at a firm leads to a 30 percent increase in total lines of code generated, a 20 percent rise in the number of total commits, and a 23 percent increase in pull requests on average, the researchers write. But all that extra code doesn’t translate directly into improved software output on the firm level. On the contrary, the resolution rate for Issues and Epics (i.e. wholesale software features) tracked by tools like Jira did not change in a statistically significant way after AI tools were introduced (the researchers also found no “compositional shift” in the size or complexity of those Jira-tracked issues across the AI introduction). The reason for that discrepancy can be found directly in the code review process, which takes markedly longer on average after the introduction of AI coding agents. Overall, the average “review process” time between a pull request getting submitted and it being merged into the codebase balloons 49 percent on average after AI agents are introduced. That effect can be seen in more granular data, too, with “the share of pull requests with changes requested nearly doubl[ing], and the number of comments per pull request increas[ing] by 35%” following the AI agent shift, the researchers write. In response to this change, the researchers found a 14 percent increase in the share of workers performing code reviews after AI agents’ introduction. They also write that they “cannot attribute significant employment changes to AI” after looking at total active workers across Jellyfish and cross-referencing with LinkedIn data at those firms. Pull requests need changes a lot more often in the “agentic coding” era. Credit: Chen and Stratton Pull requests need changes a lot more often in the “agentic coding” era. Credit: Chen and Stratton While AI could also theoretically help with this review process, the researchers found that, so far, that impact has been marginal. Although 80 percent of measured firms used some form of AI code review by March 2026, AI agents were only responsible for 23.3 percent of all review comments and 10.8 percent of all pull requests, suggesting humans were still responsible for the vast majority of this work. AI agents are still a relatively new part of the coding world, of course, and there have been significant updates and upgrades to their output even since this study’s March 2026 data cutoff. And while 95 percent of firms in the study have implemented AI coding agents by this point, many are doubtlessly still going through a learning process regarding when and how to best deploy them. These kinds of “coding time versus review time” trade-offs could improve as software engineering teams gain more experience with the pros and cons of siccing an AI agent on particular coding problems. For now, though, letting AI write your code looks like a double-edged sword, with increases in coding speed counteracted by similar increases in human code review time and effort. It’s the kind of result that makes us wonder if the considerable time and expense to get AI coding agents working is really worth it for most companies. Kyle Orland Senior Gaming Editor Kyle Orland Senior Gaming Editor Kyle Orland has been the Senior Gaming Editor at Ars Technica since 2012, writing primarily about the business, tech, and culture behind video games. He has journalism and computer science degrees from University of Maryland. He once wrote a whole book about Minesweeper . 285 Comments Staff Picks metavirus I’m forced to use AI at work and this is absolutely 10000% true. Soooooo much slop code goes into the basin, which dozens of people need to sift through, strain out the dreck, then eventually close their eyes and release into the wild because now we have new SLAs so we’re not seen as a bottleneck to progress. The game's Emotion Engine machine code is translated ahead of time into C++, compiled to WebAssembly, and linked against a reimplementation of the PS2's operating system and hardware that draws with WebGPU. Watch the full recording (1:24) This is the sibling of psp-web-recomp and follows the same method. The first title brought up this way is Gran Turismo 4, chosen because it is one of the most demanding games on the system: it leans on both vector units, on exact floating point behaviour for its replays and license tests, and on graphics tricks that read rendered images back as palettes. It plays from boot through the opening movie, the menus and races, with music and sound effects, and saves to a memory card kept in the browser. A race runs at full speed, 50 frames per second for this PAL release, in Chrome on a laptop's integrated GPU at twice the PS2's resolution, which is how the recording above was made. God of War II followed through the same scripts. It needed no game-specific code, but it found two bugs that Gran Turismo 4 had never triggered, one in the recompiler and one in the vector unit timing, and a few missing pieces of the PS2's input/output processor. It now plays from the menus through its cutscenes into combat, and holds 60 frames per second in heavy combat at the PS2's resolution in Chrome. At twice the resolution it runs at 48 to 60, limited by the laptop's integrated GPU. No game data is included here. You bring a disc image of a game you own, and the scripts in this repository turn it into a web page on your machine. How it works Recompilation. eerecomp reads the game's executable, follows its control flow to find the functions and emits C++ for them in units of 16 KiB of guest code. The output keeps the R5900's quirks: 128-bit registers and the multimedia instructions that work on them, branch delay slots, the PS2's floating point unit, which has no infinities or denormals and rounds differently from IEEE, and vector unit 0 used as a coprocessor. Jumps between units become tail calls, and a thread switch unwinds the host stack and resumes at the guest address, so the generated code never needs a stack per guest thread. A small PS2 kernel. The EE side of the operating system is answered by high-level emulation: threads, semaphores, interrupt handlers for the DMA controller and the vertical blank, alarms, and the SIF channel that connects the main CPU to the I/O processor. The I/O processor runs the game's own IRX modules, the sound driver, the disc streaming code and the controller and memory card drivers that ship on the disc, on an interpreter of its R3000 CPU, while the IOP kernel and the libraries those modules call are reimplemented in C++. The disc is read over HTTP Range requests, so only the executable is downloaded up front. Vector units. Most of a PS2 game's 3D work happens in microprograms the game uploads to vector unit 1. They run with the pipeline delays of the MAC, status and clip flags modelled, because games schedule their code around them, and with the PS2's float rules for special values: no infinities or NaNs, denormals flushed to zero and overflow clamped to the largest float. The arithmetic itself is the host's, so a result can differ from the console's in its last bit; the console truncates where the host rounds, and its multiplier is not exact. Microprograms seen during a test run are compiled ahead of time into SIMD C++; any the page meets for the first time are translated into a WebAssembly module on the spot, which takes a few milliseconds per program. Graphics. The Graphics Synthesizer's 4 MB of video memory lives on the GPU, in its native swizzled layouts, and drawing is done by WebGPU compute shaders: triangles are binned into tiles and rasterized with the GS's own rules for texturing, palettes, alpha blending, depth and destination alpha tests. Because everything stays in GS memory, effects that render into a texture or reinterpret a framebuffer as a palette work the way they do on the console. The internal resolution can be one, two or three times the native one. A software rasterizer of the same GS remains as the reference the GPU output is compared against. Threads. The emulation runs in a worker, vector unit 1 has a worker of its own the way it runs in parallel on the console, and the GS commands go through a ring buffer to the page thread, which owns the WebGPU device. Sound and movies. The SPU2 is reimplemented with its 48 voices of ADPCM, ADSR envelopes and the streaming DMA games use for music, and its output goes to an AudioWorklet through shared memory. Movies are decoded by an implementation of the IPU, the PS2's MPEG-2 decoder. Lessons from making it fast The first race ran at 3 frames per second natively, with a software rasterizer and an interpreter for vector unit 1. Moving the GS to WebGPU compute shaders and compiling the vector unit programs brought it to about 70 natively, and most of the remaining work was about where the browser spent its time rather than the emulation. The first version of the GPU renderer submitted around 650 compute dispatches per frame, because every texture upload and palette load split the batch of triangles around it. Hoisting uploads ahead of the triangles that do not depend on them, with the same output, brought that to about 80. Gran Turismo 4 uploads the same 3 MB of textures every frame of a race. GS memory is swapped between frames, so the uploads cannot simply be skipped, but a 16 MB cache of recently uploaded contents on the GPU lets most of them be served without crossing from WebAssembly to the GPU again, which cut the data sent per frame by about 60 percent. At three times the native resolution the frame rate dropped to 23. Profiling the shader showed that the per-triangle setup was being loaded after a branch that differed between threads, which made the whole setup divergent, and that uploads split into 1 MB pieces blocked Chrome's page thread. Loading the setup uniformly and writing each frame's data in one piece brought three times the resolution to 48 to 50 frames per second on the same integrated GPU. The browser's own scheduling mattered too. Nested setTimeout calls are clamped to 4 ms, so the emulation loop now yields through a MessageChannel instead, and moving the emulation into a worker, so that the page thread only feeds the GPU, steadied a race that had wandered between 40 and 50 frames per second at a constant 50. A second game God of War II went from an ISO to a page through port.sh with only generic changes, and each one was a bug or gap that the first game had simply not exercised. It started with silence. The game's sound driver drives its tick from one of the I/O processor's hardware timers, which nothing had implemented, so the driver never mixed a sample. The intro after the difficulty menu was a mess of huge flat polygons, and when the gameplay was about to begin the game crashed after its render list ran past the end of memory and overwrote its own vertical blank handlers. Following a corrupted linked list back with hardware watchpoints led to the recompiler: when a branch was the last instruction of a 16 KiB unit, the path that does not take the branch continued in the next unit at the delay slot instead of after it, running that instruction twice, or running the instruction a branch-likely should have skipped. That fixed the crash and the game reached combat, still with giant polygons over parts of the screen. Those came from triangles that should have been culled. God of War II's microcode reads the clip flags three instructions after the CLIP that sets them, and the vector unit model made them visible only after four, which Gran Turismo 4, whose microcode always waits longer, could not have noticed. Along the way it also needed a boot path like the BIOS gives, a module loaded from memory instead of the disc, and the scratchpad DMA's destination chain mode. Port a game of your own You need git, CMake, Ninja, a C++20 compiler (clang is preferred and picked up automatically), Python 3, and 7-Zip if your disc image is in a .7z . Everything has been run on Linux on x86-64. The first run installs the Emscripten SDK into tools/emsdk , or uses the one EMSDK points to, and downloads wgpu-native for the native runner. With --native-only the script skips the browser build and never installs the SDK; the native window then needs the SDL2 development files. Expect about 300 MB of disk space per game for the generated code and the builds; the disc image itself is linked, not copied. git clone https://github.com/snuri00/ps2-web-recomp.git cd ps2-web-recomp scripts/port.sh mygame " My Game.iso " python3 scripts/serve.py build/web-mygame games/mygame/disc.iso # http://localhost:8620/ port.sh takes a disc image (an ISO, or a ZIP or 7z archive holding one) and does the whole job. It reads the boot program named in the disc's SYSTEM.CNF , translates its machine code to C++, and then runs the game headless a few times. Static analysis cannot see every function a game reaches through pointers, so each run writes down the addresses it could not find, the script adds them as entry points and translates again, until a run gets through without new ones. The same runs record the vector unit microprograms the game uploads, which are compiled ahead of time as well. Last it builds the page into build/web-mygame and the native runner into build/native-mygame . God of War II goes from ISO to page in three and a half minutes on an 8-core laptop. The exploring runs press start and then cross every five seconds, which gets most games through their title screens, and put an empty memory card in slot 1 the way the page does, so they follow the path a player takes. --press 900:cross replaces that with your own inputs and --frames sets how long each run lasts. Frames from the last run land in games/mygame/shots , which is the quickest way to see how far a new game gets. scripts/build_web.sh mygame rebuilds only the page. Set your expectations accordingly: two games have been brought up so far. Another game will most likely stop at a system call or an IOP library function nobody implemented yet, which the runner logs as [sys] unhandled syscall or [iop] missing <library> #<n> , or use a GS feature the renderer does not handle yet. Browsers The page needs WebGPU for the GPU renderer. Chrome and Edge have it on Windows and macOS. On Linux it is off by default in Chrome and Chromium: turn on chrome://flags/#enable-unsafe-webgpu and chrome://flags/#enable-vulkan and restart the browser, as the page tells you when it finds no usable adapter. Without WebGPU the software renderer takes over, which is fine for menus and far too slow for 3D. On laptops with two GPUs, a canvas drawn on the discrete GPU sometimes cannot be shown on the screen; the page tries both adapters and falls back to copying frames through a 2D canvas. The keyboard maps the face buttons to Z (cross), X (circle), A (square) and S (triangle), the shoulders to Q, W, 1 and 2, start and select to Enter and Backspace, the D-pad to the arrow keys and the left stick to I, J, K and L. Gamepads work through the browser's gamepad API. Their analog triggers reach the game as the DualShock 2's pressure-sensitive L2 and R2, and controllers with motors vibrate when the game asks for it, in browsers that expose vibration (Chrome and Edge do). Phones get on-screen controls, and F toggles fullscreen. The resolution selector reloads the page at the new size. Playing natively The native runner, build/native-mygame/ps2run , plays the game in a window when SDL2 is installed; scripts/port.sh mygame "My Game.iso" --native-only builds only this one. It draws through wgpu-native on Vulkan and plays sound through SDL. The keyboard uses the page's keys for the buttons, with the arrow keys as both the D-pad and the left stick, and any game controller SDL recognizes works too, the Steam Deck's own controls included, with the same trigger pressure and vibration as in the browser. build/native-mygame/ps2run games/mygame/disc/SLUS_123.45 --disc games/mygame/disc.iso --window --memcard mygame.ps2 --fullscreen starts in fullscreen and F11 switches back and forth. PS2_SCALE=2 or 3 raises the internal resolution. As in the browser, the emulation, vector unit 1 and the GS each run on their own thread, which takes God of War II from 43 to 60 frames per second at the native resolution on the test laptop; PS2_ONE_THREAD=1 puts everything back on one thread. The memory card file uses the same layout as the page's exported cards. On a Steam Deck the runner can be added to Steam as a non-Steam game, though nobody has tried it on one yet. Saves The page puts a memory card in slot 1 and keeps it in the browser's storage for the address you play from, so progress survives a reload. Games format and use it as they would a real card. Export card downloads it as a .ps2 file in the layout PCSX2 uses, and Import card puts such a file back in the slot, so a card can travel between browsers or come from PCSX2. ?nocard starts with the slot empty. Hosting The page uses SharedArrayBuffer for its threads, so it has to be served cross-origin isolated, with Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin and Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp . scripts/serve.py sends both headers and supports the Range requests the disc streaming relies on. Anyone who can reach the server can load the game, so keep it to yourself. Legal This repository contains only original code and third-party code under its own license. It contains no game code or data. The generated C++ and the built WebAssembly are translations of the game's executable, so they belong to the game's owners: keep them on your own machine and do not publish them. Use disc images of games you own. Gran Turismo, God of War and PlayStation are trademarks of Sony Interactive Entertainment; this project is not affiliated with or endorsed by Sony, Polyphony Digital, Santa Monica Studio or any game publisher. Credits The VLC tables of the MPEG decoder are adapted from Play! (BSD 2-clause, notice in runtime/src/ipu/NOTICE ). PCSX2, Play! and the ps2sdk headers were the references for much of the hardware and system behavior emulated here. wgpu-native and Dawn provide WebGPU natively and in the browser, and Emscripten builds the WebAssembly. License The code in this repository is available under the MIT License, see LICENSE . runtime/src/ipu/tables.hpp keeps the BSD 2-clause notice of Play!. title: Fingerprints are the new cookies
body_text: Fingerprints are the new cookies â home You're protected from the methods I use here. You disabled JavaScript, so this fingerprinting trick can't run at all. You're still vulnerable to network-based methods. Read on to see what it does to everyone else. From now on Iâll call you: â¦ computingâ¦ Try refreshing the page. Clear the cookies. Connect to a VPN. Youâre still the â¦ . Now open it on your phone or some other device and your nickname will be different and just as consistent. Is it different in incognito? Good. But itâs always the same? Bad news. Imagine this: Most websites you visit get paid to show ads and indirectly run my script that lets me know youâre the â¦ . I can use it to decide what ads youâll see. But more importantly, if youâve made an account on that website, I can offer to buy your data - whatever they can share under their privacy policy: your name, activity, conversations with AIâ¦ Pretty soon Iâd know more about you than your friends do - perhaps more than you know yourself. âSo what?â - you say. âI have nothing to hide. And I prefer my ads to be relevantâ¦ sometimes they show me exactly what I need! And the data is anonymised anywayâ¦â See, the thing is, itâs not about you at all. Itâs not really about the ads anymore either. Nobody cares about you. And if the police or your government happen to care, Iâll gladly take their money too. I look at all this data and I donât see people. I see patterns. Patterns emerging out of patterns. A living, digital fractal state of the economy, society and human psyche. The crystal ball of the 21st century and itâs made of silicon! Thatâs the product. And to the highest bidder it goes! What does that make you then? A gear? An ox? A volunteer? Fingerprints are the new cookies Remember the big fuss about third-party cookies? It was so big that the EU had already rolled out one of its greatest inventions - consent banners. If EU ships faster than tech companies, that can only mean the tech companies are sitting on their hands. And one of those tech companies happens to hold two-thirds of the browser market. What was the play? Letâs give it up for Google - the biggest ad company on Earth! ACT I. PRESSURE - âPRIVACY IS PARAMOUNT TO US, IN EVERYTHING WE DO.â Itâs 2019 and the cookies are still hot. Itâs become bad PR and Safari and Firefox already block them. A year later Google pledges: we will destroy cookies!! And establish a new, privacy-first reign. ACT II. DISTRACTION - âINSTEAD OF DEPRECATING THIRD-PARTY COOKIES, WE WOULD INTRODUCE A NEW EXPERIENCEâ 5 years later: people are now preoccupied with far greater worries than cookies, and the solutions Google has developed (Privacy Sandbox) kinda suck and have raised antitrust concerns so nobody uses them. âYou know what, letâs just keep the cookies. Weâll mask your IP address* though!â (* but only when incognito while authenticated) (** in the end they didnât even deliver on that) ACT III. ACCELERATION - YOU CAN NOW USE DEVICE FINGERPRINTING IN OUR AD PRODUCTS Now thereâs a better way to know whoâs who! How does fingerprinting work? Nice, letâs nerd out properly. You visit a website. Your browser sends a request to the server and the server returns code for the browser to run. The request already reveals information about you; what browser you use, the language itâs in, the OS that runs it and your IP address, which the server needs to send you the response. That often reveals your location. Then the code runs. See, weâve made a lot of civilizational progress in making browsing safe. Long gone are the days when getting a virus just by visiting a website was a daily concern . The thing is, the definition of safety varies depending on who you ask. The broad consensus ends at isolation: a websiteâs code canât see the data stored by other websites, and it canât see your files or other applications without permission. Chrome and Edge stop here. Then you have Safari (especially on iOS/macOS 26+) and Firefox extending that definition to privacy, but they still donât fully protect you from fingerprinting. Brave and Tor are the leading privacy-first browsers, with up and coming Mullvad Browser (Mullvad being, in my opinion, one of the best VPN providers out there). The code runs on your hardware, which can be measured in ways that produce consistent and unique readings. Thereâs not much that can be done about this really, so thereâs only two established solutions: feed a little bit of noise here and there. Itâs called farbling and thatâs what Brave does to make your fingerprint inconsistent. make everything look the same, always, so thereâs no telling browser users apart. Tor and Mullvad adopt this approach. Ok, letâs create a fingerprint So there are two sources for data that can make up your fingerprint; the network request and the code environment. When you look at network, the data is generally either fragile or generic: the IP address; in a âhappy pathâ where one person always uses the same IP address, it might be the only data you need. But commonly people do a lot of browsing on mobile networks, they share the WiFi with others, they use VPNs or their home networkâs IP address is rotated by the ISP. Itâs fragile as such. headers like User-Agent or Accept-Language ; reveal your browser, OS, versions and the language set. When you can execute code on the device, you have ways to measure its hardware qualities (without any permission prompts!) and these are surprisingly stable: GPU; behaviour, vendor, driver CPU; behaviour, vendor, number of threads memory size display data; resolution, pixel ratio, refresh rate audio processing device model And on the software level; installed fonts, extensions, system infoâ¦ Millions of devices use the latest Chrome, there are millions of Macs with the M4 chip and there are millions of browsers in French. But when you look at devices that run the latest Chrome in French on an M4 , that number now drops significantly. Add to it hardware measurements and it gets so low it becomes practically unique. The fingerprint doesnât need to be truly, globally unique - it just needs to be unique enough to tell people apart in your sample size. A ZIP code (inferred from IP), a birth date (youâve given away on some platform) and sex (you fill it in everywhere) together are enough to uniquely identify over 60% of Americans. You can always add another variable to decrease the potential pool of candidates. Information Entropy Have you ever played Akinator ? You think of a character, a genie asks you some twenty questions, and somehow it knows. Thatâs fingerprinting in a nutshell, except your browser answers the questions for you. Once you understand information entropy, Akinatorâs magic turns into a simple trick. Letâs simplify with that game where you have to guess the character on a board through questions like âIs my character a man?â. If I say âyesâ, and half of the characters on your board are men, youâre now considering only half of the total candidates. Now we can say that my answer gave you logâ(100 / 50) = logâ(2) = 1 bit of information , because it cut the pool of candidates in half. The bits you get from one answer are called its surprisal: the rarer the answer, the more it tells you. a trait shared by 1 in 2 people is worth 1 bit (is a man), 1 in 8 is worth 3 bits (has a mustache), and 1 in 128 is worth 7 bits (has one eye). Surprisal quantifies the value of the answer, and entropy quantifies the value of the question. If 1 person in 128 is one-eyed, then asking about it will yield ânoâ 127 times in 128. Answer Probability Surprisal Entropy contribution Yes 1/128 logâ(128 / 1) = 7 bits 1/128 x 7 = ~0.055 No 127/128 logâ(128 / 127) = ~0.0113 bits 127/128 x 0.0113 = ~0.011 Summing up the contribution of each possible answer, the question itself is worth ~0.066 bits of entropy - thatâs the average amount of bits you gain from an answer. When we combine traits that are independent we simply add up their bits or multiply the ratios, so a man with a mustache and one eye would mean 11 bits, or 1 in 2048. Alas, as Thomas Bayes would have you know, nothing is ever so simple in practice. A mustache is already a strong indicator of a man, and a man is probably more likely to have one eye. The traits are not independent so the bits donât really add up. Some interesting applications of this type of reasoning: In medical diagnostics : A positive result from a 99% accurate test for a disease known to affect 0.01% of the population is about 100 times more likely to be wrong than you are to have the disease. You need more evidence! In cryptography : A password made out of four random words is as strong as eight random keyboard characters (but much easier to remember!) In forensic science : singling out one person in a city of a million takes about 20 bits. A witness description that matches 1 person in 1,000 provides only 10 bits, which still leaves a thousand possible suspects. So what can I do about it? Test your browser: coveryourtracks.eff.org shows you how unique your fingerprint is, with entropy for each measured data point. If youâre using Chrome youâre basically walking around with an ID on your forehead. Safari and Firefox offer some level of protection, but youâre still identifiable by advanced trackers. Brave , Tor and Mullvad Browser are the only major browsers at the moment that implement advanced protections against fingerprinting. If you donât feel like switching browsers, I get it. I am a big Arc fan myself and unfortunately itâs discontinued and will never have any privacy features. There are extensions like JShelter - they disrupt fingerprinting scripts by intercepting browser API calls. But they also break some websites. Same problem applies to Firefoxâs Resist Fingerprinting feature. The ironic truth is, privacy extensions make you more unique, since fewer people have them. So a smart tracker could detect that, ignore the signals disrupted by the extension and focus on the ones that are not. No extension can be as effective as engine-level protection built into the browser. So if you donât want to be tracked, you gotta commit. methods used on this page Iâm simply creating a hash out of a few measurements of your device. Any of these change and the hash is now different. Professional applications are much more complex than this and are able to maintain identification line when single variables change. OfflineAudioContext Renders a short tone through a compressor without playing it; tiny float differences in the result depend on your browserâs audio engine and your CPU. const off = new OfflineAudioContext ( 1 , 5000 , 44100 ); // â¦ a 1 kHz triangle wave into a dynamics compressor â¦ const data = ( await Promise . race ([off. startRendering (), timeout])). getChannelData ( 0 ); let sum = 0 ; for ( let i = 4500 ; i < 5000 ; i++) sum += Math . abs (data[i]); return sum. toFixed ( 3 ); WebGL Reads your GPUâs vendor and model (without version numbers), what the GPU and its driver support, and the pixels of a small rendered triangle. const gl = document . createElement ( 'canvas' ). getContext ( 'webgl' ); const dbg = gl. getExtension ( 'WEBGL_debug_renderer_info' ); return gpuName (gl. getParameter (dbg ? dbg. Make posters, social posts, stories, slides, invitations, resumes, thumbnails and business cards: start from a template or a blank page, edit everything, and export to PNG, JPG, SVG, PDF, MP4 or GIF. Every feature is free, nobody needs an account to start, and you can run the whole thing on your own server. 🎬 See it in action A real, unedited recording: pick a template, rename the band, recolour the dates, add a star, export. 💜 Why people pick Doory 🆓 Free, for real No Pro plan, no locked templates, no watermarks, no ads. Every tool in the editor is there for everyone, from background removal to video export. ⚡ Start in one click Open the editor and design. Guests' work is saved in the browser; create an account only when you want your designs in the cloud, and they move over in one step. 🏠 Yours to host One docker compose up runs the app, the API, the database and live collaboration on your own server. Every design and upload stays under your control. 🛠️ A real editor Layers, groups, masks, filters, curved text, snapping, rulers, multi-page designs, animation, audio, presenting, comments and real-time co-editing. 🎨 Everything you need to design Edit anything Click any text, shape or photo to change it. Fonts, colours, sizes, alignment and effects are one click away in the toolbar above the page. Bring it to life 27 enter and exit animations, 12 emphasis effects and 16 page transitions, with music and sound effects from a built-in library. Present it, or export it as a video. Stay organised Every object is a layer you can rename, lock, hide, reorder by dragging, group, or right-click to copy, duplicate, delete and arrange. Export anywhere PNG with transparency, JPG, SVG and PDF, plus MP4, WebM and animated GIF, all made in your browser. Need print? Get a print-ready PDF with bleed and crop marks. See the full feature list Text Headings, curved text, text effects, font pairings, bulleted and numbered lists, an open-licensed font catalogue and your own uploaded fonts Elements Shapes, lines and arrows, about 25,000 icons, emoji and illustrations, stickers, QR codes Photos Upload, crop, masks and filters, one-click background removal (the model runs in your browser), stock photo search with an Unsplash or Pexels key Layout Layers with lock and hide, groups, alignment guides, snapping, rulers, multi-page designs with pages of different sizes, magic resize Motion 27 enter and exit animations, 12 emphasis animations and 16 page transitions on a timeline Sound A built-in library of 24 music loops and 88 sound effects (CC0), uploads, voiceover recording, trims and fades Present Present mode with speaker notes, timing, auto-advance, a laser pointer and a second presenter window Together Share links that can view, comment or edit (optionally password protected), pinned comments, version history and real-time co-editing with live cursors Brand Brand kits with your colours, fonts and logos, one click away in every design Export PNG, JPG, SVG and PDF, MP4, WebM and animated GIF, all made in the browser, plus print-ready PDF with bleed and crop marks 🖼️ Templates that look good from the start Ten starter templates ship with Doory, each with its own palette, set in open-licensed fonts and fully editable: a gig poster, a wedding invitation, an event story, a sale post, a café flyer, a quote card, a resume, a YouTube thumbnail, a pitch deck and a business card. Add your own in the admin, and browse them all by category, size and orientation. ⚖️ Doory vs Canva Canva is a great product. Doory is for people who want the same kind of tool, but free, open and in their own hands. Doory Canva Price Free, every feature Free plan, paid Pro and Teams plans Open source ✅ ❌ Run it on your own server ✅ ❌ Design without an account ✅ ❌ Your files stay on infrastructure you control ✅ ❌ Real-time co-editing and comments ✅ ✅ Animation, video and GIF export ✅ ✅ Background removal ✅ in your browser ✅ Template library 10 starter templates, plus any you add A very large library 🚀 Self-host it in 3 commands cp .env.example .env # set DJANGO_SECRET_KEY (openssl rand -base64 48) and POSTGRES_PASSWORD docker compose up -d --build docker compose exec api python manage.py createsuperuser Open http://localhost:8080 and start designing. The web container serves the app and forwards /api and /ws to the backend, so the browser only ever talks to one address. Add the starter content (templates, icons, fonts, audio) A new site starts empty. Add whatever you want once it is running: docker compose exec api python manage.py seed_gallery # template categories docker compose exec api python manage.py sync_fonts --popular 100 docker compose exec api python manage.py seed_templates # the starter templates (add --update to refresh them) docker compose exec api python manage.py seed_elements # shapes and graphics docker compose exec api python manage.py sync_element_packs # icons, emoji and illustrations (download) docker compose exec api python manage.py sync_models # background removal model docker compose exec api python manage.py sync_audio # music and sound effects Settings worth knowing ( .env ) Setting What it does SITE_URL The public address of the site, e.g. https://doory.example.com (no trailing slash) DJANGO_ALLOWED_HOSTS The host names the site answers to, comma separated SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT , SECURE_COOKIES true behind HTTPS, false for plain http:// EMAIL_URL , DEFAULT_FROM_EMAIL SMTP, e.g. smtp+tls://user:password@smtp.example.com:587 (without it, emails are printed to the API log) WEB_PORT , WEB_BIND Where the site is published (default 0.0.0.0:8080 ) INSTALL_CHROMIUM false skips the headless browser that server-side PDF export needs GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID Turns on "Sign in with Google" UNSPLASH_ACCESS_KEY , PEXELS_API_KEY Turn on stock photo search USE_S3 and AWS_* Store uploads in S3-compatible storage instead of a local volume Develop locally make setup # virtualenv, dependencies, local database make dev-api # API on http://localhost:8000 make dev-web # app on http://localhost:5173 (second terminal) make help lists the other targets (tests, lint, content). ❓ FAQ Is it really free? Yes. There are no plans, no paywalls and no ads in Doory. Every feature is available to everyone. Do I need an account? No. Guests design straight away and their work is saved in the browser. An account keeps designs in the cloud, lets you share them and use brand kits; signing up moves your guest designs over in one step. Can I use it for my business or host it for my users? Yes, as long as you credit the author as the licence asks: keep the licence and NOTICE with it and show the credit in the running app. See License and credit . Where are my designs stored? Guest designs and their images live in the browser on that device. Signed-in designs are stored on the server that runs Doory: yours, if you self-host. Uploads can go to a local volume or to S3-compatible storage. 🧱 Built with React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Fabric.js, Yjs and Zustand in the browser; Django 5, Django REST Framework, Channels and PostgreSQL on the server; Docker Compose with nginx, optional Redis and S3-compatible storage. 🤝 Contributing Bug reports, ideas and pull requests are welcome. Open an issue to report a bug or suggest a feature. For a security problem, please report it privately through the repository's Security tab instead. If Doory is useful to you, a ⭐ helps other people find it. 📜 License and credit Doory is released under the Attribution Assurance License . title: The gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is widening
body_text: Andrej Karpathy on X: "Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel. - Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely co… / X Post Log in Sign up Post Log in Sign up Andrej Karpathy on X: "Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel. - Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come in contact with LLMs at all. - Around 1-2B (~20%) are casual and infrequent users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products. This group sees derpy chatbots and treats them a bit like a better Google search, a writing aid, or etc. Maybe an agent tries to book you a flight. I have non-tech friends who (reasonably, imo) say they have not much use for it at all. Even many professionals outside of math&code are in this tier. For example, execs and many other functions spend a lot of their time talking to other people, so while they understand what is happening intellectually, it is still second-hand and a bit abstract. - Now we get to professional use of frontier-grade LLMs in math&code. Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt. Building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries... This has all happened very quickly and recently - less than 1 year ago, I was writing code manually by hand, typing memorized computer code commands into a code editor character by character, occasionally pressing Tab to autocomplete a little chunk of code. - And finally we get to the ~5,000 people (~0.00006%) with access to frontier-grade systems internally. The external world has seen the preview. It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work. Meanwhile, human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind. For example, people are still involved in the "archeology" of the OpenAI-HF incident from many months ago. Mathematicians may be poring over the 722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics for a while. The funnel is driven by a combination of factors: 1. The impact scales with ambition, problem size, and horizon. A question with a paragraph answer barely stresses the system. You need a reservoir of big, difficult problems that you really care about. This aspect drives the consumer / professional dimension of the funnel. 2. The jaggedness of the system (which I have written about a lot separately). Capability peaks in domains that are digital, verifiable and economically valuable. This is because LLM capability emerges from reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards on a curated environment mixture driven by revenue potential. This aspect primarily drives the area (e.g. math&code) dimension of the funnel. 3. Access. Free-tier, paid-tier, internal. So this is the weirdness of the moment. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time." This has all happened very quickly and recently - less than 1 year ago, I was writing code manually by hand, typing memorized computer code commands into a code editor character by character, occasionally pressing Tab to autocomplete a little chunk of code. - And finally we get to the ~5,000 people (~0.00006%) with access to frontier-grade systems internally. The external world has seen the preview. It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work. Meanwhile, human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind. For example, people are still involved in the "archeology" of the OpenAI-HF incident from many months ago. Mathematicians may be poring over the 722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics for a while. The funnel is driven by a combination of factors: 1. The impact scales with ambition, problem size, and horizon. A question with a paragraph answer barely stresses the system. You need a reservoir of big, difficult problems that you really care about. This aspect drives the consumer / professional dimension of the funnel. 2. The jaggedness of the system (which I have written about a lot separately). Capability peaks in domains that are digital, verifiable and economically valuable. This is because LLM capability emerges from reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards on a curated environment mixture driven by revenue potential. This aspect primarily drives the area (e.g. math&code) dimension of the funnel. 3. Access. Free-tier, paid-tier, internal. So this is the weirdness of the moment. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time. Andrej Karpathy @karpathy Apr 9 Judging by my tl there is a growing gap in understanding of AI capability. The first issue I think is around recency and tier of use. I think a lot of people tried the free tier of ChatGPT somewhere last year and allowed it to inform their views on AI a little too much. title: Total Annihilation, rebuilt for modern computers
body_text: Nanolathe: an open-source engine for Total Annihilation Skip to content nanolathe Menu ＋ Get started Features Documentation About GitHub ↗ Play the demo Staged battle in Nanolathe Modern GPU renderer · Silent Play video Total Annihilation, rebuilt for modern computers. Nanolathe is an open-source engine for playing Total Annihilation on Windows, Mac and Linux. It loads the original maps, units and campaigns. You can try it right here with the three-mission browser demo. Play the demo ↗ Install the beta ▶ Watch footage 0:43 The demo needs no game files or installation. Use desktop Chrome, Edge or Safari with a keyboard and mouse. Public beta Campaign, skirmish, Survival and online play are available. Expect bugs and some compatibility gaps. A Jeffy explodes on Greenhaven The Modern renderer lights the Bulldog beside it and adds detail to the grass and trees. Drag the divider to compare with Classic. Classic CPU renderer Modern 2× art · light · glow ‹ › Both captures show the same moment at 2× zoom. Modern adds synthesized terrain and trees, lighting and glow. Captured at 960×640 in a staged scene. Classic Split Modern Capture settings and original files Captured with engine 617540c5 on October 4, 2026. This compares full renderer paths: Modern includes supersampling and its default presentation effects. The tile cache was generated from the installed game’s original 32×32 tiles into 64×64 synthesized tiles. Healthy tree sprites use 2× synthesized feature banks; shadow or missing variants retain the engine’s normal fallback. Authored dead stumps are cleared from this staged display. No screenshot cropping, retouching or resampling was used. WebP exports decode to the exact captured pixels. Open full Classic capture · Open full Modern capture More renderer comparisons Why rebuild TA? I played Total Annihilation as a teenager and got into making mods and 3D models. Years later I wanted to get it running on my MacBook Pro, and that eventually became a project to recreate the engine. Nanolathe loads the original game data directly, including the scripts that turn turrets and open factory doors. First I’m trying to match how TA works. Once that’s reliable, it’s much easier to try changes and see what they actually do. The code is written in Go and available under the MIT license. Daniel Taylor · More about the project Engine source on GitHub ↗ File formats and research Playing the beta The browser demo has three original campaign missions. For the full game, you’ll need your own installed TA folder. You can play skirmish and Survival with friends, including between desktop and browser players. Save compatibility is still being worked on. Online games don’t support saving or reconnecting yet. Installation and game files → Before you play Is this the original Total Annihilation? It’s a new engine that runs the original game’s data. Nanolathe reimplements TA through clean-room research and is an independent project, unaffiliated with the game’s owners. Do I need to own Total Annihilation? You can play the three-mission browser demo without it. For the full game, use the installed files from a copy you own, such as GOG, Steam or the original CDs. Nanolathe’s MIT license covers the engine code; TA’s artwork and other game content have separate terms. How complete is it? Single-player campaign, skirmish and Survival are broadly complete. Bugs and smaller missing features remain, and compatibility varies by mission and content pack. Skirmish and Survival battles are recorded as replays. The gameplay reference lists the systems implemented so far. Which browsers work? The demo supports desktop Chrome, Edge and Safari with a keyboard and mouse. Firefox, phones and tablets haven’t been verified. The demo downloads its game files on first launch and caches them for later visits. For larger battles, install the native beta . How do I play with friends? Choose MULTI on the main menu, create a game and send its code to your friends. Skirmish supports 2 to 10 players; Survival supports 2 or 3. Everyone needs their own game files, so the three-mission demo can’t join online games. The installed game and desktop Chrome or Edge can play together. See the online guide for rules, computer players, alliances and sharing. Nanolathe engine footage × From the announcement reel. Watch on YouTube nanolathe A spare-time project by Daniel Taylor. Play the demo About Brand kit Website source ↗ An independent, MIT-licensed engine project. Total Annihilation belongs to its respective owners. Nanolathe is not affiliated with or endorsed by them.

Preface Running Julia Edit this page Report an issue Calculus with Julia Author John Verzani Published August 31, 2026 Preface Calculus with Julia This is a set of notes for learning calculus using the Julia language. Julia is an open-source programming language with an easy to learn syntax that is well suited for this task. Read “ Getting started with Julia ” to learn how to install and customize Julia for following along with these notes. Read “ Julia interfaces ” to review different ways to interact with a Julia installation. Since the mid 90s there has been a push to teach calculus using many different points of view. The Harvard style rule of four says that as much as possible the conversation should include a graphical, numerical, algebraic, and verbal component. These notes use the programming language Julia to illustrate the graphical, numerical, and, at times, the algebraic aspects of calculus. There are many examples of integrating a computer algebra system (such as Mathematica , Maple , or Sage ) into the calculus conversation. Computer algebra systems can be magical. The popular WolframAlpha website calls the full power of Mathematica while allowing an informal syntax that is flexible enough to be used as a backend for Apple’s Siri feature. (“Siri what is the graph of x squared minus 4?”) For learning purposes, computer algebra systems model very well the algebraic/symbolic treatment of the material while providing means to illustrate the numeric aspects. These notes are a bit different in that Julia is primarily used for the numeric style of computing and the algebraic/symbolic treatment is added on. Doing the symbolic treatment by hand can be very beneficial while learning, and computer algebra systems make those exercises seem kind of redundant, as the finished product can be produced much more easily. Our real goal is to get at the concepts using technology as much as possible without getting bogged down in the mechanics of the computer language. We feel Julia has a very natural syntax that makes the initial start up not so much more difficult than using a calculator, but with a language that has a tremendous upside. The notes restrict themselves to a reduced set of computational concepts. This set is sufficient for working many of the problems in calculus, but do not cover thoroughly many aspects of programming. (Those who are interested can go off on their own and Julia provides a rich opportunity to do so.) Within this restricted set, are operators that make many of the computations of calculus reduce to a function call of the form action(function, arguments...) . With a small collection of actions that can be composed, many of the problems associated with introductory calculus can be attacked. These notes are presented in pages covering a fairly focused concept, in a spirit similar to a section of a book. Just like a book, there are try-it-yourself questions at the end of each page. All have a limited number of self-graded answers. These notes borrow ideas from many sources, for example Strang ( n.d. ) , Knill ( n.d. ) , Schey ( 1997 ) , Hass et al. ( 2018 ) , Rogawski et al. ( 2019 ) , Angenent ( 2012 ) , several Wikipedia pages, and other sources. These notes are accompanied by a Julia package CalculusWithJulia that provides some simple functions to streamline some common tasks and loads some useful packages that will be used repeatedly. These notes are presented as a Quarto book. To learn more about Quarto books visit https://quarto.org/docs/books . Compiling these notes into a pdf file with Quarto is possible with some piecing together of parts. The result is less than optimal and also quite large. Download pdf version To contribute – say by suggesting additional topics, correcting a mistake, or fixing a typo – click the “Edit this page” link and join the list of contributors . Thanks to all contributors. A very special thanks goes out to @fangliu-tju for their careful and most-appreciated proofreading and error spotting spread over a series of PRs. Running Julia For individual users Julia is installed quite easily with the juliaup utility or by other means. There are some brief installation notes in the overview of Julia commands. Specifications These are the specifications which make up modern IRC, and the extensions that the IRCv3 WG have defined. View Working Group The IRCv3 Working Group is chartered to prototype, develop and test changes to the IRC client protocol. View FAQs These are questions about IRC and the IRCv3 Working Group that we get asked regularly, and our answers. View Introduction 🔗 If you’re just getting started with IRC development, the first thing to look at would be the IRC core specifications RFC1459 and RFC2812 . One of our members has also been writing a new core protocol document here , which you may find useful to consult. After that, our specifications page contains the extensions the IRCv3 Working Group has developed. All of the IRCv3 extensions are backwards-compatible with older IRC clients, and older IRC servers. Our roadmap details the specifications we have in the pipeline, and our GitHub repository is where most of our specification work is done. For any other questions, feel free to consult our FAQ page which contains all sorts of info about us and what we do. If you’re interested in talking with us, our discussion channel is #ircv3 on Libera.Chat [webchat] . IRCv3 Features 🔗 Standardised account login using SASL to speed up registration and authentication. [3.1] [3.2] Providing the account information of other clients for the development of more advanced client features. [1] [2] [3] Optional metadata able to be attached to each message for easier, standardised extension development. [link] Instant away notifications, to let users know when other users go away or come back more quickly. [link] Showing the actual time a message was received, improving history playback from IRC bouncers. [link] Grouping related messages to simplify collapsing and display of those messages to users. [link] What We’re Working On 🔗 Standardised account registration and verification, allowing clients to provide better interfaces for end users. [link] Giving clients a standardised way to recognise, access and view chat history (provided by bouncers or servers). [link] Providing a mechanism to allow clients to automatically detect, move to, and keep using secure connections. [link] Allowing Unicode nicknames and channel names, improving the chat experience for international users. [link] Client avatars for display in graphical clients. title: Deloitte falsified documents to evade tax on Abramovich's wealth
body_text: Deloitte helped in falsifying documents to evade tax on Abramovich’s wealth, BBC finds Skip to content Watch Live British Broadcasting Corporation Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Home News US & Canada UK UK Politics England N. Ireland N. Ireland Politics Scotland Scotland Politics Wales Wales Politics Africa Asia China India Australia Europe Latin America Middle East In Pictures BBC InDepth BBC Verify Sport Business World of Business Technology of Business NYSE Opening Bell Technology Watch Documentaries Artificial Intelligence Intelligence Revolution AI v the Mind Tech Now Health Watch Documentaries Culture Watch Documentaries Film & TV Music Art & Design Style Books Entertainment News Arts Watch Documentaries Arts in Motion Travel Watch Documentaries Destinations Africa Antarctica Asia Australia and Pacific Caribbean & Bermuda Central America Europe Middle East North America South America World’s Table Culture & Experiences Adventures The SpeciaList To the Ends of the Earth Earth Watch Documentaries Science Natural Wonders Climate Solutions Sustainable Business Green Living Audio Podcast Categories Radio Audio FAQs Video Watch Documentaries BBC Maestro Discover the World Live Live News Live Sport Documentaries Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live Documents falsified to evade tax on Abramovich's wealth, BBC finds 22 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google James Oliver , Rory Tinman , BBC Panorama , Harriet Agerholm , BBC Verify and Simon Lock , the Bureau of Investigative Journalism Watch: The documents that were falsified to allow Roman Abramovich to evade tax The world's biggest accountancy firm helped in falsifying documents to hide Roman Abramovich's wealth and evade tax, BBC Panorama has found. Accounts signed off by Deloitte in Cyprus meant assets such as superyachts, mansions and private jets worth $672m (£508m) vanished from Abramovich's company accounts. Deloitte also appears to have advised on a scheme to evade a huge tax bill on the oligarch's wealth through the falsification of documents. Barrister Andrew Mitchell KC, an expert in financial services law, said Panorama's evidence showed the scheme was "straightforward" tax evasion and "it couldn't be more blatant". Roman Abramovich's lawyers said he denies that he evaded tax or concealed his fortune. They said Panorama provided no evidence he knew about, authorised or directed the falsification of any document and said it was legitimate to rely on advice from professionals. Deloitte Cyprus said it "acts in compliance with applicable laws". The findings are being revealed following a joint investigation between BBC Panorama and the Bureau of Investigative Journalism. For nearly two decades, Roman Abramovich was the most famous Russian oligarch in the UK, welcomed in London where he bought Chelsea Football Club in 2003 and bankrolled the club's most successful period. But after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, he was sanctioned by the UK government as an associate of President Vladimir Putin and forced to sell the club. Abramovich has been reported to be living in Turkey, a safe haven for him because it did not apply sanctions. In the Channel Island of Jersey, £5.4bn of his assets remain frozen and a criminal investigation has been going on for four years. The oligarch's lawyers told the BBC he denies the allegations in the Jersey investigation and says it was "undertaken for political purposes". Our investigation has uncovered new evidence about the way Abramovich's business empire has been run. It also raises serious questions about the integrity of some of his professional advisers. Getty Images Chateau de la Croe (top left) in the south of France, Fyning Hill in Sussex and two superyachts vanished from company accounts The evidence is contained in a leak that includes thousands of documents about the oligarch's finances and the operations of a network of offshore companies administered from Cyprus - which used to be a tax haven popular with Russians - between 1995 and 2022. The BBC and media partners including the Guardian, Paper Trail Media, the Organised Crime and Corruption Reporting Project, and the Cyprus Investigative Reporting Network - as well as the Bureau of Investigative Journalism - have been reporting on the leaked files since 2023 as part of the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists' Cyprus Confidential investigation. In 2022, Panorama also reported on how Abramovich had made his fortune from a corrupt deal to buy a Russian state-owned oil company in the 1990s, selling it back to the government a decade later for billions in profit. He has previously said allegations of corruption in the deal are false. The profits from Abramovich's oil deals in Russia were funnelled into a web of offshore companies. They were administered from Cyprus by a corporate services firm called MeritServus, in Limassol, the island's second-largest city. Until 2005, Deloitte - now the biggest of the "big four" firms which dominate the accounting industry - owned MeritServus. After they split, the two companies worked closely together with Abramovich's associates to manage his global fortune. The leaked documents from MeritServus reveal some of their practices. Our first example of backdated paperwork comes in 2006, after a new law in Cyprus meant that company accounts had to be made public. The new transparency law threatened to expose the secrets of Abramovich's vast wealth. Deloitte Cyprus had prepared draft accounts for 2003 - but had not yet finalised them - for his Cypriot company Amiscan Investments. The accounts detailed $672m of luxury property. A mansion in West Sussex, a luxury flat in London and an estate in the south of France were all included - plus helicopters, private jets and a small fleet of boats the oligarch owned at the time, including the $147.5m Pelorus. Deloitte in Cyprus appears to have advised Abramovich's company on a scheme to evade tax To keep them secret, Abramovich's associates and Meritservus decided to rewrite history. They drew up a plan to circumvent the transparency law by transferring the assets to Amiscan's parent company in the British Virgin Islands (BVI), where they could be kept hidden. And they backdated the change by three years to make it look like the asset transfer had happened in 2003. Deloitte Cyprus reviewed the backdated documents and said they were "adequate" to allow them to remove the assets from Amiscan's accounts. When the 2003 accounts were signed off by Deloitte in 2006, the homes, planes and yachts disappeared at the stroke of a pen. Only $75,000 of assets remained. Deloitte signed off the accounts even though the leaked documents show it knew they were completely misleading. Lord Sikka, professor of accounting at the University of Sheffield, said it was a "violation of a statutory duty" and "pretty scandalous" to misrepresent transaction dates and not to publish true and fair accounts. Panorama also found evidence that backdated documents had been used in a tax evasion scheme. This involved another one of Abramovich's Cypriot companies, Kravin Investments, which had almost $2bn in the bank in 2003. It had been earning large amounts in interest, so Roman Abramovich's company should have been paying tax on that interest to the Cypriot authorities. But his advisers had another idea to rewrite history. Abramovich's close associate misled UK court in £1bn oil-fields case, documents suggest An email from MeritServus in August 2005 to Abramovich's Russian associates said a plan had been devised after a meeting with Deloitte. "If you agree, it will be necessary to change the financial statements and the accounting records accordingly for 2003 and 2004," the email read. MeritServus informed the oligarch's Russian associates, that Kravin's "Provisional Tax Assessments for 2005" would be filed showing the company earning no income from the money. A month later, an associate in Russia emailed in response, "I agree". MeritServus then created a series of backdated documents which falsely purported to show that Kravin was only holding and investing the funds on behalf of its parent company in the BVI. This made it look like Kravin did not actually own the money, so it would not be liable for tax in Cyprus. Deloitte wrote in a September 2005 email that "certain changes will have to be made to the accounts (bank account balances, interest income, profit and loss account)" because of the backdated changes to Kravin's assets. So Deloitte was apparently advising on the falsification of financial records. The evidence suggests it allowed Abramovich's company to evade millions in tax. Andrew Mitchell KC told us the scheme was "straightforward" tax evasion. "If it happened in England and it was in the millions, His Majesty's Revenue and Customs would be thinking about a prosecution," he said. Cypriot MP Christos Christofides said that if tax had been evaded, then "we have to see how we can get our money back and how, if some people are guilty, they have to pay the price according to our law." In addition to the documents which Deloitte helped to backdate, Abramovich's advisers at MeritServus falsified a third set of records. This involved the oligarch's huge business fortune - more than $10bn - held by a company called Electus Investments in Cyprus. MeritServus backdated documents to make it look like Electus did not own the fortune. It used another Abramovich company with exactly the same name of Electus Investments, but this time based in the more secretive BVI, where accounts did not have to be made public. Emails show that in 2006, MeritServus acknowledged that the fortune was owned by Electus Cyprus. But again it proposed to rewrite the past, this time "to transfer the beneficial ownership to Electus Investments in the BVI" and make it look as though the change had happened three years earlier. MeritServus signed and backdated documents which falsely purported to show the BVI company had owned the $10bn fortune since 20 November 2003. So when the accounts of the Cypriot company with the same name were made public, it appeared to have assets worth just $145,000. Roman Abramovich's billions had been made to disappear. Andrew Mitchell KC told Panorama: "What you take away from it is there are professionals who are prepared to bend and break the rules of their profession and therefore the law. And it looks that they will stop literally at nothing in terms of creating documents." Vladimir Milov, Russia's deputy minister of energy as Abramovich built his empire and now a critic of the Russian government, said: "For each Russian oligarch or Middle Eastern or African corrupt oligarch, there's an army of Western financial and legal services and PR services providers, who is easily taking money for whitewashing their reputation and making them look normal." Denying any wrongdoing by the oligarch, Roman Abramovich's lawyers said that he was "not involved in the day-to-day operation of those companies" and that where arrangements were proposed by professional advisers, "reliance on that advice was entirely proper and legitimate". Deloitte Cyprus said it could not comment on the specific allegations because the documents were more than 20 years old and no longer accessible. MeritServus closed following the Cyprus Confidential leak. Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. Sign up here.
