Because mobile Linux is no longer isolated and locked into silos controlled by large companies, such as Nokia, Samsung, LG, Mozilla and Canonical, it has a much greater chance of succeeding and attracted contributors than it did in the past. Because Phosh and Plasma Mobile and Sxmo are based on using existing software stacks that are maintained by outside organizations, they are much less likely to be abandoned, as happened with Firefox OS, or to ossify and fade into obscurity, as happened with Hildon. PINE64’s attempt to get around the cost of developing software PINE64 was founded as a crowd-funding campaign in October 2015 by TL Lim and Johnson Jeng to develop a single board computer based on the Allwinner A64 processor. The company based in Hong Kong focuses on producing economical Linux hardware devices. It gets around the high costs of developing software by just producing the hardware and then invites the community to develop the software for its devices. By allying with various different Linux distros, PINE64 initially had a great deal of success. PINE64 probably shipped over 100,000 PinePhones , which greatly stimulated the development of mobile Linux. The release of the PinePhone led to the creation of the Mobian ( Mob ile Deb ian ) and DanctNIX (based on Arch ARM) distros and inspired the creation of the Sxmo interface. The PinePhone helped Plasma Mobile decide that it only needed to run on a Linux stack and pushed UBports to add support for running on a Linux kernel. It also caused many of the major distros to work on porting to a mobile device for the first time. PINE64 played an important service for the community by getting cheap hardware into people’s hands so they develop software for that hardware, but it made the fundamental mistake of focusing on the distros, which only works if the hardware already has kernel support and good free/open source drivers. Drew DeVault, the lead developer of Sway and one of the volunteer developers who worked on the PinePhone, observed that PINE64 was putting the cart before the horse, by helping to finance the packaging work in particular distos, rather than first paying developers to work on the booting and driver development, that would have benefitted all the distros. Because PINE64 chose hardware for the PinePhone that was mostly already supported by FOSS drivers, it was able to attract a large number of distros to work on the phone. Volunteer developer Ondřej Jirman (aka “mega” or “megi”) created a custom Linux kernel for the PinePhone. Volunteers at UBports did the initial work on bringing up the hardware. Arnaud Ferraris (aka “a-wai”) at Mobian developed the telephony stack using the eg25-manager in userspace. Martijn Braam at postmarketOS worked on the camera. PINE64 initially released a series of five development batches of the PinePhone, which had different distros preinstalled (Ubuntu Touch, postmarketOS with Phosh, Manjaro with Phosh, Manjaro with Plasma Mobile and Mobian with Phosh). For each phone sold, PINE64 donated $10 to the distro which provided the software. After that, PINE64 planned to let the buyer select which distro to support by selecting the distro’s logo to display on the back plate of the PinePhone’s case. Nonetheless, there were arguments among the different distros behind the scenes over the design of the hardware projects. PINE64’s founder, TL Lim, grew frustrated and decided to just ship PINE64’s devices with one distro and one interface preinstalled. Given the complexity of trying to work with so many different distros, this wasn’t an unreasonable decision, but it had to be handled with care to not alienate the other distros. Unfortunately, Lim chose to only ship PINE64 devices with Manjaro and Plasma Mobile preinstalled. PINE64’s own poll of PinePhone users showed that Phosh was the most popular interface, but it was controlled by Purism, a competitor to PINE64. Plasma Mobile wasn’t a bad choice, since it was a community-based interface that needed corporate support. Manjaro, however, was a very poor choice, since it wasn’t doing any software dev work and has been widely criticized for its bad practice of shipping software in development that is known to be broken, which creates more work and public backlash for the projects developing the software. Many of the crucial volunteers who worked on the PinePhone were burned out by the time that development on the PinePhone Pro started. They were frustrated by the internal arguments and the fact that PINE64 had shifted from sharing revenue with many distros to only paying Manjaro, rather than the people who were doing the necessary dev work. The PinePhone Pro’s hardware required quite a bit of software dev work to support it. In August 2022, Martijn Braam at postmarketOS publicly broke up with PINE64 due to its bad decisions in favor of Manjaro. PINE64’s response failed to address Braam’s frustrations, and Drew DeVault posted that “ PINE64 has let its community down .” Most of the volunteer developers stopped collaborating with PINE64, so the community-based company didn’t have the manpower to do the necessary software development for its new hardware. Most distros weren’t willing to work on a phone that couldn’t even properly boot. Thousands of people bought the PinePhone Pro after it was released in December 2021, expecting that eventually it would become a functional device, but it still had major software problems when its sales were cancelled in August 2025. The failure of the PinePhone Pro illustrates that PINE64 had its priorities backwards by focusing on one distro that mainly does packaging work, rather than focusing on the booting and kernel work. Another of the problems was that PINE64 sent out its free hardware samples to the same small number of volunteers. By the time that the PinePhone Pro started its development, those volunteers were overwhelmed by all the new hardware that PINE64 was releasing, which all needed serious software dev work to ever be functional. With so many projects needing attention, the volunteers couldn’t focus their energy on any one device, so all of them got neglected. PINE64 charges such low prices for its hardware, that it doesn’t have the necessary funds to pay for serious software dev work. However, its revenue sharing model with the distros was working to convince talented people associated with those distros to do the hard work of supporting its hardware. Then, PINE64 undermined its whole community development model by deciding that it would only sell its hardware with one distro and one interface preinstalled, and its decision to only share its revenue with that one distro. Then, PINE64 made matters worse by only listening to Manjaro in how it designed its hardware, which alienated many of the volunteers from other distros that it needed to do the software dev work. Once the best volunteers abandoned PINE64, the company hasn’t been able to complete the development of the PinePhone Pro, PineNote, PineTab2 and many of its other projects, so the people who ordered these devices are unlikely to ever be able to use them as fully functional devices. Rather than sharing revenue with many different distros, PINE64 should have used any profits that it generated to pay developers to work on the drivers and kernel support for the hardware. It could have taken a community-based approach by observing who was making progress, and helping to finance their work. Because the Allwinner A64 already had decent free/open source drivers, volunteers were able to fill in the gaps with the PinePhone. However, many of the kernel changes that they made never got upstreamed to mainline Linux, which PINE64 could have required if it were paying for that work. PINE64 also could have directed its revenue sharing program to help finance development work that would benefit all users of PinePhone, regardless of which distro they chose, such as Martijn Braam’s work on the Megapixels camera app or Biktorgj’s work on freeing the EG25-G modem firmware . Given that Phosh, Plasma Mobile, Lomiri and Sxmo/Swmo were being packaged in many different distros, it would have been better to pay people to work on developing those mobile interfaces than giving money to the distros. There are plenty of volunteers in the community who were willing to work on porting distros to the PinePhone, but there are far fewer people who are willing to do difficult driver and software dev work in their spare time. The waning enthusiasm for Linux phones After the initial enthusiasm for the Librem 5, PinePhone and PinePhone Pro in 2020-21, there was a noticeable drop in people’s interest in Linux phones. The number of posts about the Librem 5 and PinePhone on Reddit and the Purism and PINE64 forums reduced in 2022-25. The subsequent announcements of new Linux phones, namely the F(x)tec Pro 1 X with Sailfish OS and Ubuntu Touch, the Volla phones with Ubuntu Touch, FuriLabs FLX1/s/s+, the Jolla C2 with Sailfish OS, Liberux NEXX, Commodore Callback 8020 and Mecha Comet, haven’t generated nearly as much public interest and community engagement as the announcements of the Librem 5, PinePhone and PinePhone Pro. This difference is partly due to the fact that Purism and PINE64 were established companies that were already shipping Linux devices and they had community forums and Subreddits where people could gather and discuss the upcoming devices. Nonetheless, I suspect that many of the people who bought the Librem 5 and PinePhone had a similar experiences to mine which dampened their enthusiasm for Linux phones over time. When both of those phones first arrived, they were fascinating devices for geeks like me, who had been playing around with Linux for years on their desktop PCs. I had a blast flashing different distros on the PinePhone and I frequently downloaded the latest version of PureOS and reflashed my Librem 5. I ran benchmarks on the two phones and eagerly followed the dev work to add support for the phones’ hardware. I had spent years waiting for the Librem 5, and after it arrived, I followed the development of Phosh and Adwaita by the Purism developers, like I was rooting for my favorite sports team. I considered the development of Phosh and Plasma Mobile to be the most exciting thing that was happening in the Linux world, and I enjoyed trying out new versions of the interfaces to see what was new in each release. The first year after the Librem 5 and PinePhone were released were exciting times. I was so intrigued by the phones that I looked up every component on the Librem 5 and PinePhone schematics and documented them on the projects’ wikis. However, each time I flashed a new distro on the PinePhone to try it out, I only played with the phone for a day or two, before it went back in the drawer on my desk. I took the PinePhone apart and admired how it was designed, but I never used the phone for very long before I put it down. Its performance was poor. It took a long time to load apps and there was a noticeable delay in the interface. I also found it distracting to use the phone when the screen was dimmed or the battery was low, because of the noticeable flicker on the screen. I considered pulling out the soldering iron to implement a fix that would speed up the Flash memory storage, but I feared that I might accidentally ruin the board. I expected that PINE64 would issue an new version of the PinePhone that would fix the problems, but instead PINE64 dismissed the screen flicker as a problem and hasn’t changed the eMMC’s voltage from 3.3 to 1.8 volts, which would have increased its sequential read speed from 55 to 125 MB/s . I was also annoyed that PINE64 provided no way to communicate with its hardware developers, so I wasn’t able to get errors fixed that I found in the PinePhone schematics. Unlike the Pinephone which I rarely used, I kept using the Librem 5, because its better CPU and memory performance made its interface much more responsive than the PinePhone. Nonetheless, the Librem 5’s screen and aluminum frame got hot, since Purism used thermal paste to join the i.MX 8M Quad to the LCD’s backplate to dissipate the processor’s heat through the screen and aluminum frame. I often felt like I was walking around with a heater in my pocket. The battery drained fast, so I was constantly having to charge the Librem 5. Eventually the Purism developers got the Librem 5’s camera to work, and I tried out each new version of the Millipixels app. It was fun playing with the camera and I learned a lot about how cameras work trying to adjust the settings to get a good photo. However, the Librem 5 took a long time to process each photo in software after taking a picture, since its i.MX 8M Quad processor lacked an image signal processor and hardware encoder in the VPU. It also took me way too long fiddling with the Millipixels’ settings for me to rely on the camera. Whenever I wanted to make sure that I would get a decent photo, I pulled out my Xiaomi Redmi Note 7 running LineageOS to take the photo. Eventually it was possible to shoot video on the Librem 5 at a low resolution and frame rate, but it took so long to process the video and the quality was so limited, that I never bothered using it. In the end, the PinePhone sat most of the time in a drawer in my desk, and the Librem 5 sat charging on my desk. They were good entertainment for the geek in me, but I didn’t use either of them as my primary phone. Many of the early adopters appear to have had similar experiences with their Linux phones. It was hard to justify buying another Linux phone, when there was already one sitting unused in the drawer. Many people were unwilling to take a chance on another Linux phone after witnessing how the community developers abandoned PINE64 in 2022, and software development stalled for the PinePhone Pro and how Purism refused to refund cancelled orders for the Librem 5. When FuriLabs announced its upcoming FLX1 in June 2024 , it solved many of the problems with the Librem 5 and PinePhone. It contained a 6nm MediaTek Dimensity 900, which was powerful enough shoot video and run 3D games with Vulkan . It offers three hardware privacy switches and multi-booting to run multiple operating systems on the phone. The phone’s software was developed by Bardia Moshiri, who is the lead developer of Droidian , which runs Phosh in a Debian-based distro on top of Halium with an Android kernel. It was based on well-supported projects and software which had already been developed, so its costs would be low, but it had an experienced developer to provide software support. In other words, it would avoid the high costs that troubled the Librem 5 and the lack of software support that bedeviled the PinePhone Pro. People report that the FLX1 and its following FLX1s and FLX1s+ variants work well, but the Linux phone is not well-known and appears to have gotten a limited number of orders. The company’s forum has been frozen and there has been limited activity on the Droidian forum , indicating that the phone has gained little traction in the Linux community. Revision 1.1 of the Divine D. circuit board arrived on Aug 10, 2026 . In January 2025 , Liberux, a startup based in Madrid, Spain, announced its upcoming NEXX Linux phone based on the RK3588S with specs to make nerds salivate: 4×2.4GHz Cortex-A76, 4x Cortex-A55, Mali-G610 MP4 GPU, 32GB LPDDR4X RAM, 256GB eMMC, 5G modem and 3 hardware kill switches. In June 2025, Liberux started the crowdfunding for the phone, and a couple days later announced a modular and open architecture that would allow the RAM board with an FPC connector to be upgraded up to 32GB, the eMMC board with a standard socket to be upgraded up to 512GB, and the cellular modem with a custom adapter board to be replaced/upgraded. The price varied between €790 and €1310, depending on the selected configuration. In addition, the NEXX would have two USB-C 3.1 ports to facilitate the phone being used a convergent desktop PC and an AW8737SCSR amplifier and a 3.5mm audio jack for better analog audio. The NEXX was a revolutionary design, promising to be the first phone in history with two USB ports and the first one with the RAM and eMMC on separate boards, so it could be upgraded and connected like a normal PC. Liberux was attempting to offer the first truly convergent smartphone that had the right software and hardware to replace a desktop PC, yet it hardly generated any headlines in the tech press. It only got 120 pre-orders in a month, which generated a tenth of the $1.7 million in crowdfunding that it needed. When its crowdfunding campaign failed, Liberux reported that it was negotiating with investors for raise the funds to build a prototype. However, its last post on the company’s Mastadon account was in November 2025 about “moving forward with new self-funding.” After 11 months of silence, it is looking increasingly doubtful that the NEXX will ever come to market. There is more hope for the Dawndrums Divine D. phone, which is being produced by a startup in Tunisia. The startup has continued to make slow progress according to its Mastodon posts . They are now on the second revision of their main board and have produced a breakout board for debugging it. They are developing their own distro known as DawnOS , which is based on Mobian and planning to support both the Phosh and Plasma Mobile interfaces. They are asking for donations , but appear to be largely self funded at this point. Like the NEXX, the Divine D. also promises to be an outstanding convergent phone, supporting up to 32GB RAM and offering a separate HDMI port for video out. It also offers a LoRa (long-range radio) chip, and a pogo pin interface to add accessories to the phone. Jolla shows that there is still demand for Linux phones While the failed crowdfunding of the Liberux NEXX and the limited sales of the FuriLabs FLX1 would suggest that there isn’t much hope for Linux phones, it is important to keep in mind that these phones were poorly advertised and produced by unknown startups that had no prior track record, so people were reluctant to order them. Bitter experience with the Librem 5 refunds, the failures of the PinePhone Pro, and all the cancelled Linux mobile devices over the years, such as the Ubuntu Edge in 2013, the Firefox OS phones in 2015, the Jolla Tablet in 2015 and the Necunos NC_1 in 2019, has taught Linux enthusiasts to be cautious about crowdfunding mobile devices. However, there are reasons to believe that there is quite a bit of pent-up demand for mobile Linux, and it only requires the right kind of promotion and a company with a credible track record to unlock it. Ironically, the company demonstrating that people still want to use Linux phones is tiny Jolla , which has somehow managed to survive over the years. The Finnish engineers who used to work on Nokia’s MeeGo founded their own company named Jolla Oy in 2011 to keep developing that code as Sailfish OS. They took the FOSS parts of MeeGo and added their proprietary Silica interface based on Qt QML , which imitates the Swipe UI that Nokia had developed for MeeGo on the N900/N9 . They also licensed the proprietary Alien Dalvik from Myriad Group to run Android apps inside Linux, and now markets it as AppSupport , which has been updated to run more recent versions of AOSP in an LXC container. Jolla deserves credit for developing libhybris and helping to maintain much of the code developed by Nokia, including the oFono telephony library and the Maliit virtual keyboard. Remarkably, the small Finnish company managed to survive nearly going bankrupt in late 2015, when it cancelled its crowdfunded Jolla Tablet , and was only able to return half of the money to the customers who pre-ordered the tablet. After killing off the original company in 2024, because it was majority owned by Russian investors, who were politically toxic due to the war in Ukraine, Jolla reemerged under a new company named JollaBoys that bought the old company’s assets from Jolla Oy. The new Jolla company has returned to the business of selling hardware. Jolla announced its Jolla C2 Community Phone in May 2024 , and started delivering them four months later , which helped reestablish the credibility of the company. When Jolla started taking preorders for its new Jolla Phone on December 5, 2025, it sold out its crowdfunding goal of 2000 phones within the first 48 hours and 5000 phones within the first week. People were pre-ordering the Jolla Phone without having seen any reviews of the phone and not even knowing what processor it would contain. The phone, which initially cost $499 and now costs was €679, was marketed as containing 12GB RAM, 256GB storage, a user-replaceable battery and a physical privacy switch. Jolla’s advertising for the phone clearly struck a chord with European consumers, which proclaimed it to be a “Do It Together (DIT) Linux phone, shaped by the people who use it.” The Finnish company emphasized the independence of the phone from the rest of the mobile phone industry, stating on the order page: “The Jolla Phone is not based on Big Tech technology. It is governed by European privacy thinking and a community-led model.” Jolla has sold 15,000 units of its phone as of August 2026 just by taking pre-orders for production batches from its web site, and it probably could have sold far more units if it had paid for advertising, expanded beyond the European market, and kept the phone in stock, so customers didn’t have to wait months for the next production batch. Clearly, there is an untapped market of people who are dissatisfied with the reigning Android/iOS duopoly. The mobile industry is shutting down the AOSP alternative Today the use of Linux is growing on the desktop. Many people are installing Linux on their PCs, because they have become disgusted by how Microsoft has turned Windows into an advertising platform for surveillance capitalism and a vehicle for AI slop. Rather than buying new PCs, a growing number of people have decided to install Linux, because support for Windows 10 has ended and they can’t upgrade their old PCs to Windows 11 due to Microsoft’s arbitrary TPM restrictions. Likewise, many people are equally disenchanted with Android and iOS on their phones. More people have grown distrustful of the surveillance capitalism which undergirds the Android market and the restrictions and rising prices of Apple’s “walled garden” on the iPhone, yet the options to escape the smartphone duopoly keep shrinking. In the past, people who wanted to gain some control over their digital lives could unlock the bootloader on their phone and install an AOSP derivative such as LineageOS, /e/OS, CalyxOS or GrapheneOS, however the mobile phone industry is increasingly shutting off this escape valve. Every year there are fewer Android phone models on the market which allow the bootloader to be unlocked. The rise of Chinese brands, which now control roughly 60% of the global smartphone market, has driven many of the traditional phones brands out of the market which did allow their bootloaders to be unlocked. Many of the phone brands that were mod-friendly, such as LG, BQ, LeEco, WileyFox, Essential and Razer, are now gone from the market, and other mod-friendly brands like Sony and HTC now have so few sales that they are no longer relevant in the global smartphone market. Huawei stopped allowing its bootloaders to be unlocked in 2018. In the last couple years, Samsung, ASUS and Realme all followed Huawei’s bad example and no longer allow their bootloaders to be unlocked. Xiaomi, which rose to fame as a mod-friendly brand, has recently implemented so many restrictions to obtain its unlock codes , that it is unlikely that modders will bother porting custom ROMs to future Xiaomi models. As noted in my article on LineageOS statistics , the brands which have good policies for bootloader unlocking has shrunk from 42.5% to about 7% of the global smartphone market over the last couple years. The brands which allow their bootloaders to be unlocked (without major restrictions like Xiaomi) only sold about 87 million phones in 2025, including Lenovo/Motorola ( 60M ), Google ( 12M ), OnePlus ( 11.6M ), Nothing ( 2M ), GigaSet ( >1M ), Sony ( 400k ), Fairphone ( 145k ), SHIFT ( 10k ), Teracube, Volla and Brax. Together those brands only represent 7% of the 1245.5 million total smartphones sold in 2025. However, that is an overestimate, since most phone models never get good custom ROMs made for them. A good portion of Motorola and Google phones are sold through carriers, and many carriers like Verizon don’t allow their phones to ever be unlocked, even if they are no longer under contract. MediaTek Dimensity and UNISOC Tiger processors have gained market share in recent years, and those chipmakers don’t publish the source code for their kernels like Qualcomm does for its Snapdragon processors. A few brands that use MediaTek SoC’s, such as Motorola, Xiaomi, Volla, Gigaset, TeraCube and Brax, do publish their kernel code, but that code for many other MediaTek phones will never get published, nor will custom ROMs be made for them. UNISOC processors are basically black boxes for the modding community. The bootloaders of all phones with Apple A-series, Huawei Kirin and recent Samsung Exynos processors are locked, so the modding community is restricted to just Qualcomm Snapdragon, Google Tensor and some MediaTek Dimensity processors. Motorola and Xiaomi have switched most of their budget model lines from Snapdragon to MediaTek Dimensity processors, so they are harder to mod. Aside from the Motorola Moto G05, which was released in Jan 2025 and replaced 8 months later by the G06, there has not been a single budget phone released by a major phone maker in 2025 or 2026 that has gained official support by LineageOS. Gaining official LineageOS support is important, because many of the other custom ROMs are based on LineageOS and only port to its officially supported models. Just looking at phone models with official LineageOS support which allow their bootloaders to be unlocked, only about 20 million or 2% of smarphones sold each year are good for installing custom ROMs. The situation is about to get much worse. Sadly, Oppo just announced that it will pull its OnePlus brand from the North American and European markets. OnePlus phones will still be sold in India and China (where the bootloader can be unlocked if the user presents an official Chinese ID card), but OnePlus is essentially gone for the modding community. Nothing, which was a rising star in the modding world, has been losing sales. The London-based company denies rumors that it will pull out of a third of the countries where it currently sells phones, but confirms that it plans to cut 100 jobs, which comprise 12% of its workforce. At any rate, none of the phones which Nothing has released in the last two years have gained official LineageOS support. Samsung has been making it more and more difficult to mod its phones over the last decade, so the Korean company’s decision to lock the bootloader for all its phones getting its ONE UI 8 interface wasn’t a surprise, but Xiaomi’s decision to start restricting its bootloader unlock codes was a major blow for the modding community. The only major global brand left for modding is Motorola, but there are only unofficial ports available for recent Motorola models, meaning that some things don’t work correctly or security patches aren’t being provided. Motorola promises to launch phones with GrapheneOS in 2027, but they will be flagship models which probably cost over $1000 and be limited to a few select countries. Aside from the Motorola Moto G15 (released in December 2024), people are unlikely to find a new phone where they can install an official LineageOS port for sale in Africa, most of Latin America (except Mexico) and most of Asia (except India, Japan, Taiwan, Singapore and Malaysia). The only option to run a custom ROM in most of the world is to buy a used Motorola or Xiaomi phone from a couple years ago, such as the Moto G (2024), Moto G32, Moto G34, Moto G84, POCO F5, POCO F5 Pro, POCO F6 Pro or Redmi Note 13 Pro. There are more recent phones like the Moto Edge 70 , which have unofficial LineageOS ports, but it is a gamble if they will ever be officially supported by LineageOS. As Google has pushed phone makers to support their phones for longer, many companies have decided to collect more personal data from their users for better targeted advertising and for training artificial intelligences. The smartphone industry is moving away from a business model based on planned obsolescence toward one based on surveillance capitalism, and the phone makers don’t want their users to opt out of the system, so they have removed the option to unlock the bootloader and made it harder to gain root access. That way they can recoup the cost of providing more years of support for their phones by monetizing their users’ data. In addition, Google has made it harder to maintain custom ROMs, because it has moved more and more functionality from AOSP into its proprietary libraries and services (starting with Android 4.1 in 2012), and largely abandoned the development of many of the free/open source apps in AOSP in favor of its proprietary apps. Starting with AOSP 16 in 2025, Google stopped including the device trees and driver binaries for Pixel devices in AOSP, so ROM developers no longer had target devices, where they could easily test out and adapt the latest versions of AOSP on running hardware. Now custom ROM developers have to do painful trial and error to make the device trees for Pixel phones just like all the other phone brands. Google also squashed the kernel’s commit history, which makes it very difficult for ROMs like GrapheneOS to create their own custom kernels, because they can’t easily take new features, bug fixes and security patches from Google’s kernels. Given how the smartphone industry is locking down their hardware and pushing business models that are inimical to users’ privacy, there is increased opportunity for Linux phones to be marketed to people who want to escape the Android/iOS duopoly and surveillance capitalism. Three types of Linux phones are now possible In the past, it was much harder to bring a Linux phone to market, but now there are three viable types of Linux phones that can be brought to market, and all of them have better prospects than in the past. The first type is the pure Linux phone which runs a Linux kernel, like the Librem 5, Liberty, PinePhone and PinePhone Pro. These phones previously didn’t have the processing power to offer the functionality that people expect in a smartphone. They often lacked components such image signal processors, audio digital signal processors, hardware video encoders, Vulkan graphics, neural processors and encryption engines, or they lacked the FOSS drivers to support those components. The RK3588S and the upcoming RK3668 , however, will give pure Linux phones the processing power to be viable alternatives to Android and iOS phones for the first time. The pure Linux phone is the riskiest type because it requires the most investment in engineering the hardware. Companies can’t just modify a reference phone design from Qualcomm or MediaTek or call up a phone ODM and ask them to modify one of their existing designs. They have to work with a design house or ODM that has some experience with radio frequencies to custom design a phone with 2 to 3 times more components than a standard smartphone. This means many iterations of the circuit board to get it right, and some kernel work to use all those different chips. It will take a long time to get to market, which can lead to customer complaints and reputational loss if using crowdfunding to finance the dev work. The benefit of the pure Linux approach is that it allows for true hardware kill switches that cut the current to separate components, rather than the use of pins on an integrated mobile SoC or software to turn off the WiFi/Bluetooth, cellular modem and GPS/GNSS. The second benefit is the ability to select components that have free/open source drivers, which allows for greater software freedom and more transparency to address security and privacy concerns. The use of proprietary blobs in the drivers often prevents the kernel from being upgraded because the blobs are often only compatible with a specific kernel version number, which allows the chipmakers to dictate the lifespan of devices. Another benefit of not using a reference design from an SoC maker or an ODM is the phone maker has full control over the design and can publish the schematics and board views for the circuit boards, so the hardware is as free as the software. In the past, Qualcomm didn’t produce powerful Internet of Things processors with Linux support, but now it is possible to build a good Linux phone based on an Internet of Things processor, like the QCM6490 or QCM8850 with an integrated cellular modem. These Dragonwing processors are not as up-to-date as the latest Snapdragon processors, but most of them receive 10 years or 15 years of software support, and many of them will eventually get partial support in mainline Linux, so they can live on with community support after they are no longer supported by Qualcomm. The third kind of Linux phone is built on an integrated mobile SoC, which runs a standard Linux stack on top of an Android kernel using libhybris to translate glib calls to Android’s Bionic. This used to not be a good option because Android SoC’s were not supported long enough for the long development cycles and lower annual sales of Linux phones, but now it is possible for the high-end processors that are getting 8 years of software support from Qualcomm and MediaTek. This approach is the most economical way to bring a Linux phone to market, since many phone ODMs already have reference models available and are willing to work with phone sellers to tweak those models to their specifications. It is not impossible to work with an ODM to add privacy switches to a design, as FuriLabs demonstrated with its FLX1, but it takes longer to get a custom design to market, so it is important to select an SoC that gets 7 or 8 years of software support, so the phone will enjoy a reasonable lifespan. It is no longer necessary for Linux phone companies to expend huge amounts of capital in developing mobile Linux, because there are now three good mobile interfaces—Phosh, Plasma Mobile and Lomiri—which offer a reasonably complete complement of applications, so hardware companies don’t need to risk bankruptcy developing the software like before. Because Phosh and now Plasma Mobile are based on a well-supported desktop stack and convergent applications, they will require much less work to maintain and it is easier and less costly to keep providing software updates for the phone. Companies offering Linux phones will still need to hire developers to work on things like power management and camera support, but they don’t have to bet the farm like Purism did with the Librem 5 or provide no software support as PINE64 did with the PinePhone and PinePhone Pro. The shorter software support for the QMC4490 and the mid-range and low range Snapdragon and Dimensity processors rules out the making of an economical Linux phone. It is possible to make an upper mid-range Linux phone based on a Snapdragon 7 or Dimensity 8000 series processor, but it won’t support video out via DisplayPort Alt Mode over USB-C, so it can’t be used as a convergent PC, which is a major selling point for Linux phones. Given that the QMC6490 does support DisplayPort Alt Mode, it is probably the best option for making an upper mid-range phone. Companies like Jolla, FuriLabs, Volla and Brax may choose to continue making mid-range Linux phones, but they will likely suffer from the same problem as the FLX1 and C2, where the Android kernel is unsupported and no longer getting security updates, so it is better to move up to a more expensive SoC that gets 8 years of support. Ideally, these companies will stop using MediaTek processors, and select Snapdragon processors that get partially supported in mainline Linux, so people can run a distro like Nura on them after they are no longer supported. The real barrier holding back Linux phones is the companies Now that the available SoC’s and software are no longer holding back the making of compelling Linux phones, the real barrier to creating a viable Linux phone market are the companies to make and sell those phones. There aren’t many companies with the experience and passion to make Linux phones, which historically have lost money. PINE64 recently announced that it is pausing production of most of its devices due to the high prices of RAM and eMMC. Essentially PINE64 is admitting that it can’t raise the price of many of its products, because they don’t have the needed software support, so many people won’t pay elevated prices for them. It appears unlikely at this point that PINE64 will change its business model to pay for software developers to work on the kernels for its hardware, nor is it repairing its relationship with the distributions and volunteer developers who have abandoned the company, so it is unlikely to ever produce the rumored PinePhone 2 using the RK3566. In theory another community-based Linux hardware company could arise, that charges a bit more so it has the necessary funds to pay developers to work on the kernel support for the hardware, but it appears highly unlikely that another community-based hardware company like PINE64 will appear. In contrast, Purism is clearly planning to produce a second version of its phone. In its July 2026 newsletter, Purism stated that it “is in the early stages of planning the Librem 5 v2 and Liberty 5 v2.” It is preparing a “crowdfunding campaign in the coming months” to “gauge customer interest and traction, which will help fund the production of our second version.” The problem is that Purism’s public reputation has been stained by its refusal to refund the Librem 5 backers who cancelled their orders. Refunding the 600 customers who are still waiting for their Librem 5 refunds would do a lot to restore the company’s public reputation, and it would cost the company less than $400k. Without taking that step, it seems unlikely that Purism will be able to crowdfund the “over $2 million” that it projects will be needed to produce its next Linux phone. Maybe Purism can charge a lesser amount (such as $99) to pre-order the phone, and then use those numbers to raise capital privately to develop the phone. At any rate, the time and cost of producing the Librem 5 v2 will be much less than the first version of the phone, because Phosh and its applications have already been developed and the mainline Linux driver support for the RK3588S is already in a good state due to the last four years of work by Collabora. Hopefully, Purism will either provide funding or developers to help Collabora get the ISP and hardware video encoding working. The challenge for Purism is that it also needs to finance the development of its next generation of Librem 14 notebook, Librem 11 tablet and Librem Mini. The Librem 11 and Mini are rebadged ODM designs, so they don’t require as much work, but the Librem 14 is a custom design, which requires quite a bit more work and financing to create. In addition, Purism reported in its July newsletter that it has been pre-approved to get over $50 million in funding from the CHIPS Act to develop a Librem Core-V processor based on the RISC-V architecture, which will be a huge undertaking for the tiny company which doesn’t have any prior experience in chip design. Presumably, Purism will have to raise some matching funds to get the government funding for its chip project. In other words, many projects will be competing for Purism’s attention in the future, and the Librem 5 v2 could be neglected and postponed in favor of other products. Presumably Dawndrums will launch a crowdfunding campaign once it has a working prototype of its RK3588S-based phone to show to the public, but the company based in Tunis has been very tight lipped about its future plans to bring the phone to market. There has been no news from FuriLabs about a new phone model to follow the FLX1s+. The implementation of Ubuntu Touch on the BraX3 phone has been stalled for months , and it appears that Brax Technologies is depending on the UBports community to finish the porting work. Volla Phone continues to offer Ubuntu Touch as an alternative operating system on its phones, but the German company’s primary focus is on developing its own Volla OS , which is an AOSP derivative oriented toward privacy. Jolla is making the right moves to create a viable Linux phone market. The Finnish company says that it plans to move to mass production of its Jolla Phone, so the phone will be in stock, and to offer the phone to the North American market. However, many in the Linux community will be reluctant to embrace Jolla’s phones, because of the proprietary software in its Silica interface and its AppSupport (aka AlienDalvik) to run Android apps. People who believe in free and open source software won’t want to buy a phone from a company that has been violating the GPL 2.0 license by not published the kernel code for its Jolla C2 and Jolla Phone. In addition, these phones use UNISOC and MediaTek processors that don’t have any mainline Linux support, and they will probably have short lifespans, since their kernel are unlikely to ever be upgraded. A critical factor in the success of Linux phones is publicizing the phones to attract the niche customers who care about Linux, software freedom, privacy or security. Liberux appears to have failed because it did such a poor job of publicizing its future NEXX phone and didn’t attract enough crowdfunding. FuriLabs similarly has done a very poor job of publicizing its phone, so that most Linux enthusiasts have never heard of the phone. Likewise, Dawndrums has done a very poor job of publicizing it development work on a future RK3588S phone. In contrast, Jolla has very effectively used social media to market its Jolla Phone to European customers. There are several dozen companies that sell Linux PCs, which could potentially expand into the Linux phone market. Most of those companies, however, don’t have experience in the design of custom hardware. Most of them use standard notebook designs from one of the ODM’s that make specialty notebooks such as Clevo or Tongfang. Most of these companies also don’t have much experience doing kernel work, so they are probably better off just using a standard Android design provided by a phone ODM and installing Linux on top of Halium, so they can use a well-tested Android kernel and drivers. There are also a number of companies that make Linux single board computers (SBC’s), who could potentially jump into the Linux phone market. They have more experience in working with Chinese and Taiwanese companies to design and produce custom hardware. They are better equipped to undertake the engineering challenges of entering the Linux phone market, but most of them do a poor job of engaging the community. Many companies which sell Linux SBC’s don’t have public forums for their customers and do a poor job of using social media and online advertising to promote their products. Public opinion surveys show that people are increasingly aware that they are losing their privacy online. Ipsos polls found that 79% of global respondants and 84% of American respondants express worry about their online privacy. A Malwarebytes survey found that 89% of consumers are concerned regarding corporate and AI data misuse. 62% of Americans in a YouGov poll report worrying about how much personal data third parties have about them online. If Linux phones can be created that provide the same functionality and ease of use as Android or iOS phones, they could tap into that huge potential market of consumers who wish to preserve their privacy online. In order to appeal to mainstream users, Linux phones will need to support the usage of Android apps through Waydroid or a similar solution. In the same way that Murena and iodé sell AOSP phones which block third party trackers, Linux phones need to incorporate similar software. The conditions may be ripe for Linux phones, but it is unclear whether the companies selling Linux phones will take advantage of those conditions to create a viable alternative to the current Android/iOS duopoly. For the sake of software freedom, online privacy and the greater longevity of mobile devices, a concerted push is needed to promote mobile Linux. title: The tilde in your PATH may not be your HOME
body_text: The tilde in your PATH may not be your HOME Disconnect3d's blog About me Links Tags My talks My talks (v2) The tilde in your PATH may not be your HOME 2026-10-02 • shell , bash , zsh , security I was playing with the nono agent sandboxing tool and it greeted me with a warning: PATH entries the sandbox can write to: ~/.local/bin/ which looked suspicious. In other words, doing this in your ~/.bashrc or ~/.zshrc : export PATH = " $PATH :~/.local/bin/" will not expand the ~ (tilde) into the home path (or $HOME ) as the tilde to home expansion happens only in unquoted inputs, as also the bash documentation says : If a word begins with an unquoted tilde character (‘~’), all of the characters up to the first unquoted slash (…) are considered a tilde-prefix. (…) Bash checks each variable assignment for unquoted tilde-prefixes immediately following a ‘:’ or the first ‘=’, and performs tilde expansion in these cases. (…) So instead of having /home/<user>/.local/bin/ added to PATH we end up with ./~/.local/bin/ added to PATH . And to fix this, we can do this: export PATH = " $PATH : $HOME /.local/bin/" Note that the unquoted version export PATH=$PATH:~/.local/bin actually works in Bash and Zsh, because tilde expansion is also performed in variable assignments after = and after each : . But relying on that is fragile as for example, a whitespace will break the variable assignment. The problem can also be seen here: $ ls -la total 0 drwxr-xr-x@ 2 dc staff 64 Oct 2 13:37 . drwxr-x---+ 105 dc staff 3360 Oct 2 13:37 .. $ mkdir -p ./~/.local/bin/ $ printf '#include <stdio.h>\nint main() { puts("hello"); }' > a.c ; gcc a.c -o ./~/.local/bin/kek $ PATH = "~/.local/bin/" kek hello $ tree -f . ├── ./~ │ └── ./~/.local │ └── ./~/.local/bin │ └── ./~/.local/bin/kek └── ./a.c 4 directories, 2 files As we can see, the kek binary was found and executed from ./~/.local/bin/ — the home directory was never involved. Check your PATH You can quickly check whether you have this problem with: $ echo " $PATH " | grep -- '~' or, to see each entry on its own line: $ echo " $PATH " | tr ':' '\n' | grep '~' ~/.local/bin/ If it prints anything, go fix your .bashrc / .zshrc / .profile and replace the ~ with $HOME :). Btw, kudos to the nono tool for warning about this - even though the warning could be more verbose (PR incoming). title: The Lightbulb Computer
body_text: The Lightbulb Computer: Reimagining Spatial & Ambient Computing with Projectors The Lightbulb Computer published September 2026 · Guillaume Ardaud A video version of this piece is available on YouTube . Modern visions for the future of human-computer interaction are excessively focused on smart glasses and headsets - devices that are constraining & socially awkward. This project explores an alternative direction - a speculative device called the Lightbulb Computer that uses modern projector technology & computer vision advancements to blend ambient computation & spatial information display in everyday spaces. In this series of design prototypes, I want to share with you a direction for computing that involves projecting information in the real world to augment it, rather than keeping it confined to small rectangular screens, or worse - piping it through devices that live on our faces. I call this vision the Lightbulb Computer: a device that combines a projector with computer vision, in the shape of a large lightbulb. The lightbulb form factor means it can easily be mounted in a small portable lamp-like base to carry it around the house; or screwed into any wall or ceiling Edison socket, for a room-scale permanent setup. Mounted in a portable battery base, the Lightbulb Computer can easily be placed anywhere on a desk, or around the house.   Not only is the ceiling a great vantage point to view the entirety of a room and project anywhere; lightbulb sockets are a near-ubiquitous worldwide standard. The Lightbulb Computer reacts to voice commands; sees where you point; can analyze what it sees; and can project content and highlight things in the real world. Use Cases Here are some things you can do with this device: In the kitchen, you can pin widgets like recipes and timers, or overlays to help with mise en place , on various surfaces:   It's a much more natural way to get things done, especially with wet hands, or hands covered in flour. You don't have to unlock your phone, dealing with a tiny screen full of notifications and distractions. When studying or reading, you can ask questions about the content: You get the answer right there, without having to pull out your phone, and potentially get distracted by something else. When planning a trip with someone, rather than huddling around a phone, you get a giant map to look at things together, with basic gestures to pan & scroll the map; you can toggle transit overlays, and check out all the sights you want to see. Of course you're still free to use your phone if you want to look up something that requires typing or more complex interactions, but it's just a much more convivial experience to be looking at a big map together like that. Similarly you can send photos over from your phone and have them projected on any surface. It's a much nicer way to look at photos together. I think these sorts of social interactions really shine with the Lightbulb Computer. You might even play board games - perhaps less fun than with a physical board game, but much quicker to set up, with nothing to tidy after, or worry about kids or cats knocking over tokens. Interacting with smart home devices also becomes much more fluid - you can just point to control them. If you have more than a few smart home devices, you know it's impossible to remember their specific names, but the Lightbulb Computer can just see what you're pointing at, and make those interactions much more natural. You could also use the Lightbulb Computer to have an ambient display - for example next to your bed, showing the time, your alarm clock, the weather or calendar for the next day - again all without having to stare at a screen. A shared family board can live in the hallway, where everyone can see it at a glance; items can be checked off just by tapping. What's really nice about this is that it just blends into your environment, and isn't another screen in your house. Modern vision models can read information in the world in milliseconds, much faster than we can; it'd take me at least a few minutes to go through all the books on these shelves, or I can just ask: Other physical objects in the house can also be augmented by the Lightbulb Computer. This beautiful 3D map of the area around my house can be overlaid with the weather, or customizable, time specific information, like conditions at my favorite ski stations during the winter: It can also make the map interactive: I can ask it to highlight the location of a little mountain village I forgot the whereabouts of. All the videos shown here are from a real - yet bulky - prototype setup. No video editing or special effects, or AI generation. And while I don't think the technology is quite there yet to build a consumer version of this Lightbulb Computer today, I also don't think we're too far off. Computer vision has improved tremendously recently; and projector technology is steadily advancing, with bright, high resolution, small footprint projectors now being a reality. User privacy would naturally have to be a first-order consideration for such a device; that can be addressed through existing best practices like on-device processing, hardware guardrails against unauthorized camera access (camera only turns on when activated by the user, with a hard-wired indicator light; physical cover; etc.), and so on. I think in light of the alternatives that the industry is pushing right now, it's a path for the future of computing really worth pursuing. Imagining a New Horizon for Spatial & Ambient Computing Today we have two very distinct ways of interacting with information. On one hand we have the physical objects that we've had for centuries: books, maps, printed pictures, physical tools; on the other, we have computing devices: laptops, phones, tablets - in short, screens. Recently screen-based computing has attracted a lot of criticism: for being addictive; for being antisocial; for offering us a very reductive view of the world. When we're interacting with a screen, we're not really interacting with the broader physical world: we’re limited to a small pane of glass, that encourages us to ignore what's around us. There’s been a new vision for computing, that I will call "eyewear-based computing". It also gets called Virtual Reality; Mixed Reality; Augmented Reality; and more. Fundamentally, it all involves putting something on your face, in front of your eyes. And that's already a weak proposition: it might interfere with your hair, makeup, jewelry, existing optical aids like glasses or contacts. Not only that, but the eyewear form factor is constrained in many dimensions for computing: the device has to be very small and lightweight which means strong limitations on power, computation, thermals. And maybe most important of all, it feels fundamentally antisocial. Everybody is required to have their own device, and those devices need to be compatible with one another for any shared experience. This is the kind of image you’ll often see in marketing materials. But really if you were to enter this room, this is not what you would see. This is what you would see: So while eyewear-based computing is interesting in some respects, I don’t think it addresses the deeper problems we have with screen-based computing - and this is where projector-based computing becomes much more compelling. There’s a long history of using projectors for computing: in research and academic projects (see e.g. I/O Bulb , LuminAR ); in products like the Humane Pin; community projects like Dynamicland or Folk Computer (which use projector-based computing to reinvent people's relationship to computing); and more broadly in installations in museums and public spaces. But none of those cover what we would call personal computing: the kind of things that we do today with laptops and phones and tablets, especially in our homes, or at work. And that's where I think there's room for real reinvention. ✾ Thanks for taking the time to read all the way through - if this is a vision you think is exciting, definitely reach out and let me know what you think. There are more demos I haven't shown here, and if there's interest I can share that - as well as some behind the scenes of how I got these prototypes up and running. About the author Guillaume Ardaud is a French/​American software & interface designer based in Tokyo since 2023. Worked for Apple as a prototyper/​designer for over 8 years on projects like Face ID, Apple Pencil, and the iPhone camera system; since 2022 has been independently designing and consulting as Héliographe . If you want to chat more about this project, or any hardware/​interaction/​software design projects in general, get in touch !

title: Build your own decision model
body_text: Build your own decision model Mastodon Another Dev's Two Cents Home Mastodon Bluesky By Nish Tahir — 10 Oct 2026 Build your own decision model "System one" decision models are models that infer and respond with calibrated probabilities or every allowed answer. Consider your everyday language model, to get typed output from it (JSON), you may use Structured Output to constrain the output to guaranteed valid JSON. While model prefills the input in one pass, it still has to go perform a pass for every token in order to generate a valid response. In this example, 11 passes are required to generate the final output. (We're not accounting for speculative decoding and other inference optimization techniques.) Step Play Reset prompt (prefill) generated (predicted) being predicted This interactive example needs JavaScript. Decision models such as Jev , make the assumption that there are fixed options we can select from and we can do so quickly by making a single pass. In this example we constrain the set of possible outputs to the options A , B , C , D , E . By masking other items in the vocabulary, the model can only emit those tokens. By selecting the highest probability output, we get our answer. Step Play Reset prompt (prefill) generated (predicted) being predicted This interactive example needs JavaScript. Since the outputs are constrained to only a fixed set of options, the model can't select anything outside of those. This however does not guarantee that the output will be correct. It's also common to treat the output token probabilities a confidence scores in this context, but without additional training, those scores likely reflect its confidence in what the next token will be rather than the true probability of the response being the correct answer. Build your own We can emulate this behavior by constraining output tokens using an LLM. Here I'm using Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B import argparse import json import torch from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer model_name = "Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B" options = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E"] parser = argparse.ArgumentParser() parser.add_argument("--input", default="question.json") args = parser.parse_args() # load the tokenizer and the model tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name) model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( model_name, torch_dtype="auto", device_map="auto" ) # the token the model would emit for each option as the first assistant token option_token_ids = [tokenizer.encode(opt, add_special_tokens=False)[0] for opt in options] def format_prompt(item): prompt = item["question"] + "\n" for opt in options: prompt += f"{opt}. {item[opt]}\n" prompt += "Answer:" messages = [ {"role": "user", "content": prompt} ] return tokenizer.apply_chat_template( messages, tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True, enable_thinking=False ) with open(args.input) as f: item = json.load(f) model_inputs = tokenizer(format_prompt(item), return_tensors="pt").to(model.device) with torch.no_grad(): logits = model(**model_inputs).logits[0, -1] # constrained decoding: only the option tokens are allowed probs = torch.softmax(logits[option_token_ids].float(), dim=-1) print(f"prediction: {options[probs.argmax().item()]}") for opt, prob in zip(options, probs.tolist()): print(f"{opt}: {prob:.4f} {item[opt]}") Running it with an simple question to test it yeilds the following output // input { "question": "What color is the sky?", "A": "Red", "B": "Blue", "C": "Green", "D": "Purple", "E": "I don't know" } // output prediction: B A: 0.0000 Red B: 0.9988 Blue C: 0.0000 Green D: 0.0000 Purple E: 0.0012 I don't know The model was able to make sense of our input and make a prediction that reasonably corresponds to the correct answer. We can test the accuracy of the model by running it against public datasets. I ran this against a random sample holdout of CommonsenseQA precision recall f1 support A 0.5733 0.7197 0.6382 239 B 0.5506 0.7686 0.6416 255 C 0.5372 0.6598 0.5922 241 D 0.7206 0.3904 0.5065 251 E 0.7519 0.4255 0.5435 235 accuracy: 725/1221 = 0.5938 macro f1: 0.5844 Not bad for a 1.7B model, Running a quick finetune on the dataset gives us slightly better performance precision recall f1 support A 0.6475 0.6611 0.6542 239 B 0.6113 0.6784 0.6431 255 C 0.6234 0.5975 0.6102 241 D 0.6700 0.5418 0.5991 251 E 0.5808 0.6426 0.6101 235 accuracy: 762/1221 = 0.6241 macro f1: 0.6234 Calibrating your model Testing the model against a very ambiguous problem demonstrates an interesting problem. // input { "question": "Where would you most likely find a bat?", "A": "Cave", "B": "Baseball game", "C": "Attic", "D": "Zoo", "E": "Sporting goods store" } // output prediction: A A: 0.9978 Cave B: 0.0004 Baseball game C: 0.0017 Attic D: 0.0000 Zoo E: 0.0001 Sporting goods store There should be no clear answer here, but treating the output probabilities as a pseudo "confidence" score, shows that the model is extremely overconfident in this answer. If we bin the confidence score ranges in the eval I ran earlier, we can see that the model's confidence does not match its accuracy. This means that the model is not calibrated . bin count confidence accuracy (0.00, 0.10] 0 0.0000 0.0000 (0.10, 0.20] 0 0.0000 0.0000 (0.20, 0.30] 3 0.2834 0.0000 (0.30, 0.40] 26 0.3761 0.2692 (0.40, 0.50] 41 0.4538 0.2683 (0.50, 0.60] 70 0.5490 0.3286 (0.60, 0.70] 74 0.6476 0.3649 (0.70, 0.80] 77 0.7495 0.4286 (0.80, 0.90] 121 0.8555 0.4711 (0.90, 1.00] 809 0.9855 0.7009 We can notice that the model tends to be extremely overconfident in the 0.9 - 1.0 bin but it's only correct 70% of the time. When it makes a prediction with 0.8 - 0.9 confidence it's only accurate ~40% of the time. This means that the model is generally overconfident in its predictions. Since our goal is to have the model output scores that is reflective of its accuracy, one method we can use to callibrate it is through temperature scaling. By modifying the temperature value, we can flatten its output probability distribution curve and scale it to approximate its accuracy. temperature T This interactive example needs JavaScript. Curve fitting fit the temperature parameter to the model's accuracy, I found 3.797280788421631 as a temp value. bin count confidence accuracy (0.00, 0.10] 0 0.0000 0.0000 (0.10, 0.20] 0 0.0000 0.0000 (0.20, 0.30] 82 0.2712 0.2317 (0.30, 0.40] 217 0.3507 0.3917 (0.40, 0.50] 199 0.4472 0.5126 (0.50, 0.60] 166 0.5475 0.5482 (0.60, 0.70] 139 0.6562 0.5827 (0.70, 0.80] 140 0.7492 0.7714 (0.80, 0.90] 169 0.8507 0.7988 (0.90, 1.00] 109 0.9333 0.9541 This gets us a much better calibration. If you want to play around with this, I made a GitHub repo with scripts that walk you through building a dataset, evaluating, finetuning and calibrating your own model. I encourage pulling it and trying it on other bigger models. title: Sharing AI progress in mathematics
body_text: Sharing AI progress in mathematics | OpenAI Skip to main content Research Products Business Developers Company Foundation (opens in a new window) Log in Try ChatGPT (opens in a new window) Research Products Business Developers Company Foundation (opens in a new window) Try ChatGPT (opens in a new window) Login OpenAI October 6, 2026 Research Publication Sharing AI progress in mathematics View on GitHub (opens in a new window) Loading… Share We’re releasing a broad range of new mathematical results produced by an internal frontier model . As we look to improve how we share results with the math community, we’ve been consulting with the independent Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence at the Institute for Advanced Study ⁠ (opens in a new window) to develop best practices, and we have drawn on their advice and public recommendations ⁠ (opens in a new window) to inform how we release these results. For this release, we’re publishing the results in a GitHub repository, with protocols for paper revisions and citations. We’re continuing to explore other community-hosted alternatives for this release which meet the committee’s guidelines. For future releases, we are committed to further improving the quality of the papers via the citations, mathematical exposition, and presentation of the results for better understanding. As part of our GitHub repository, we are sharing formalizations of many of the proofs in Lean, a programming language that allows mathematical proofs to be checked by a computer. We will update the repository with more formalizations as we obtain them. To promote scientific transparency and openness, we are also publishing additional details about how we obtained the results in the repository. These include 10 summaries of the model’s reasoning, estimations of compute spent in terms of Pro usage on ChatGPT, and statistics about the number of attempted problems. The average result used the equivalent compute of roughly three hours of ChatGPT Pro thinking. We want this progress to push the frontier of human knowledge and enable further progress in mathematics. We will be funding a series of workshops, conferences, and special programs around the understanding of major results produced by AI—we will share more on this in the near future. We want to directly empower scientists with state-of-the-art capabilities and are working to responsibly release the model that produced these results. This is why it is important to continue to evaluate our internal frontier models on mathematics and other sciences, so we can accelerate developing the tools to advance those fields. We will continue to act on feedback from the community and update our standards for future disclosures of major scientific advancements. 2026 Author OpenAI Keep reading View all An OpenAI model proposes a solution to the Navier–Stokes problem Research Sep 8, 2026 Ten advances in mathematics and theoretical computer science Publication Aug 1, 2026 Accelerating scientific discovery with ChatGPT for Academic Researchers Company Jul 29, 2026 Research Research Index Research Overview Economic Research Latest Advancements GPT-6.1 Sol GPT-6 Astra GPT-5.6 GPT-5.5 Safety Safety Approach Deployment Safety (opens in a new window) Security & Privacy Trust & Transparency Products ChatGPT (opens in a new window) ChatGPT Business (opens in a new window) ChatGPT Enterprise (opens in a new window) ChatGPT for Education (opens in a new window) Codex Dots (opens in a new window) Release Notes API Platform Overview API Log In (opens in a new window) Docs (opens in a new window) Business Overview Solutions Resources Plugins Customer Stories Partner Network Contact Sales Developers Apps SDK (opens in a new window) Open Models Docs (opens in a new window) Resources (opens in a new window) Developer Forum (opens in a new window) Company About Us Our Charter Careers News Support Help Center (opens in a new window) OpenAI Status (opens in a new window) More Stories Academy Supply Co. title: Sorry, I'm in a meeting
Grieving the loss of details
body_text: Grieving the loss of details | purplesyringa's blog purplesyringa about blog kitchen sink Grieving the loss of details September 24, 2026 Lobsters Hacker News I’ve been thinking about where I stand in respect to the current state of the industry. This is more of a journal note than a post, apologies for that. I usually leave this stuff private, but I thought I’d post this as a trial in case someone relates to this experience and feels less alone. All opinions are my own. Before the term “vibecoding” was coined and the industry shifted to valuing programmers primarily for designing architecture, I proudly called myself a coder as opposed to an engineer. In my eyes, this highlighted the way I focused on the details, performance optimization, knowing the intricacies of the language, and being able to explain how things work, as opposed to juggling Java-esque abstractions. Of course, this was partially a misconception, but I can’t help but notice how the opportunities to use my strongest sides are getting away, and the industry is switching to a model my mind is incapable of working with. I first became familiar with computing when I saw the history scene in Tron: Legacy : 10 year old me needed to know what these lines meant, and so I began the grueling job of learning programming. I didn’t care about practicality, building useful programs, or writing code per se: all I wanted is to understand how the machine works . It took several years of learning and maining Linux until I figured it out, but I got there. Later, I tried specializing in different areas, like networking, cryptography, or Rust, but I always found myself gravitating towards the machine itself. I learned to appreciate it and respect its wishes. I found joy in writing a toy OS, counting cycles, and writing machine code by hand. I took pride in inventing clever hacks. Like a fisherman might feel one with a fishing rod, I treat the machine as a continuation of myself. I’ve been doing this for eight years now, and I’m way in over my head. I hesitate to switch CPUs because I don’t understand ARM64 as well as I understand x86, and that genuinely gives me discomfort. I worry about allocations in Python code. I’m deeply concerned about not knowing how to look at JIT disassembly of Java code running on my PC. Today I found an annotated version of The Story of Mel and caught myself thinking, who could possibly need “hexadecimal” explained? I don’t see myself as a programmer who is also an expert in a niche area; I see myself as exclusively a low-level coder, or even just a detail-oriented person. I can make a website if I have to, but I can’t work on it for a month straight the way I can on low-level software – but I can very much research physics the same way. My focus on details doesn’t end on technology. I can’t learn topics top-down or deal with absent information. When someone explains a concept to me, I need to reinvent it myself from scratch until I “get it”. In school, I would spend hours adjusting axioms for my intuition until they fit, and then building theorems on top of them every time I needed to use them, until they, too, became intuitive. (Hell, my and my girlfriend’s quality time is often proving theorems.) Closer to reality, I can’t experiment with cooking without understanding the underlying chemistry. Generally speaking, I can’t use something I don’t understand completely – if it doesn’t click, I can’t work with it. This is genuinely debilitating in day-to-day activities, but for a while, the software world was the one reprieve I had from this struggle. Even those who didn’t get would at least respect my work on low-level projects. There was an understanding that minor optimizations in compilers compound, that someone needs to write assembly for JSON parsers to go brrr, and that programs don’t have to suck the way Electron slop does. Maybe it wasn’t the central part of software development, but it was important enough that investing some time in it was considered worthwhile. In other cases, I built reputation by knowing stuff, the way I could glance at people’s issues and know what went wrong. That lasted until powerful LLMs came out. The overwhelming consensus across the industry is that LLMs will make such a draining and exhausting process as “worrying about details” obsolete, and let developers focus on abstractions and large projects. Great for them, but I’m not exaggerating when I say they took everything from me. If anyone can point an LLM at slow code and it automatically finds a hot loop and uses a trick it found somewhere on the 'net to vectorize it, there is little point in hiring someone with a focus on that. If an LLM can analyze the code and explain pointer provenance to you and babysit you until you get it, there is little value in expertise. I cannot use LLMs this way. I get almost physically ill when I work on a project with more source code files or at least general architecture than I can keep in my head, so I don’t get anything out of expanded scope. Last time I tried using an LLM for a pet project, I realized that the LLM would come to know more about it than pretty much any person I could show it to. I can be content with being a misunderstood genius, or whatever – but being not just deemed unworthy of human interaction, but effectively shown the door and redirected to an LLM is beyond insulting. I swore not to use LLMs for anything I care about since then. Over the course of a year, I went from having a planned future to worrying about applying for disability. LLM-driven development optimized out every part that makes programming bearable for me, the job market decided it’s the future, and now that the one option in my life I thought constant disappeared, it turns out there there was never a decent alternative. That’s where I stand for now. Aside from big tech, which is greeting LLMs with wide arms, few companies have resources to care about the type of work I do. Linux had a chance to be an exception, but oh well. Hobbies still exist, but they don’t pay the bills, and increasingly retrocomputing and performance optimization are being infested by LLM fans that seek recognition rather than the experience, which sucks the fun out. Made with my own bare hands (why.)

title: Why isn't the industry freaking out about DeepSeek 4.1 Flash?
body_text: Why Isn't The Industry Freaking Out About DeepSeek 4.1 Flash? Skip to main content Jono's Corner Top level navigation menu Home Posts About Feed Why Isn't The Industry Freaking Out About DeepSeek 4.1 Flash? 07 October 2026 tech I have been using DeepSeek 4.1 Flash for about a month, heavily, across a dozen projects. It is super capable, and orders of magnitude cheaper than the "frontier" models. When I'm mid-session, if I don't look at the model name, I honestly could not tell you if I'm using DeepSeek or Opus. Whether it's our conversations, the work, or the speed, I don't notice a difference. I don't care that there is no 4.1 "Pro". I treat this like a frontier model because it behaves like one . I'm coming at this from my subjective usage experience, but you can see more complete benchmarks here if that floats your boat. So why aren't the frontier labs freaking out right now? China is going to eat their lunch. They may be a month or two behind Anthropic/OpenAI, but these distilled Chinese models can handle the same workloads. Sure, they stole Claude's training , and Anthropic stole it from other people. I'm not getting into the whole who-owns-whose-data debate, because most developers aren't thinking like that. They're just trying to get the most bang for their buck. Good Enough Changes How You Work Today's models are now good enough for high-quality unattended tasks. Chasing the latest and greatest is silly. It is fun to see the new Fable capabilities, but the tasks we throw at them are usually ridiculous (maybe even insulting) if you believe in LLM sentience. It's like asking a math PhD to organize the files on your desktop. With my OpenCode Go sub of $10/month, DeepSeek is basically unlimited. This has completely changed my way of developing. There is no shame now in spinning up mindless tasks, or exploratory UI monkey testing. And sure, go ahead and reorganize your desktop files. That will cost $0.003 instead of $1. I have rarely exceeded $1 in expected costs in a session. I try to keep my sessions tight, but sometimes they run for most of a day. I even lean on 4.1 Flash for complex planning and research. For occasional critical tasks , I sometimes pull in Opus 5.5 to do a final code review, which will catch a few edge cases. Then I have DeepSeek execute the fixes. Even when I call up Opus or GLM (which seems to be drinking the same Chinese Kool-Aid as DeepSeek), it's less about quality and capabilities and more about getting new eyes on a problem. Cache Magic DeepSeek shrank the KV cache by roughly 437x compared to their V1 model. Holding that cache in GPU memory is one of the biggest costs of running long coding sessions. That's how my all-day sessions stay under a dollar. It must be better for the environment too. Using Claude almost feels wasteful, and not just on cost: its caching means DeepSeek must be using less water and electricity. This cache magic is also how Opus 5.5 quietly got its own efficiency boost. Yes, I have frontier subscriptions. My work provides Claude, Cursor, and others. I'm not nickel-and-diming here. I'm thinking more about long-term planning, sustainability, and democratizing access to high intelligence. This is a game changer. These wins are lost on the tech industry, which thinks that if you're not paying top dollar, it's not worth it. FAANG wants to spend the most money for the highest intelligence. Forget it if it's unethical, expensive, or bad for the environment or the economy. This is dog-eat-dog capitalism. This leads to people having crazy setups to load balance a dozen Claude Max subs , and complaining when they can't get more . And to the self-hosters out there, the economics of 4.1 Flash mean self-hosting is not worth it. If saving money is your goal, you will never recoup the costs. But if your concern is privacy, just wait. These cache optimizations are coming to you, and this cache magic will soon run entirely locally. Even now, 4.1 Flash is technically self-hostable, even if not practically so. Any day now. PS Welcome, good people of HackerNews . Seems like we hit a nerve 😃 My point here is that these Chinese companies are playing by different rules, and soon more models will be following suit. The frontier labs have an entirely different business model, and they need to recoup the high cost of training these new LLMs. This is like comparing big pharma with generic manufacturers who can skip the R&D. While these drugs are not one-to-one copies, this is close enough to comparing apples to apples, but with a 90% price cut. ← Previous AI DevEx Log - July 2026 Built with eleventy

2026, 16:07 Save for later Save for later Add as a preferred source on Google Follow on Google News A man has decided to buy his parents a new coffee maker after discovering their smart machine broadcast a massive 1TB of data in just 10 days. Going by Nomad, the man shared his discovery on X after checking their parents’ network activity and finding that their coffee maker had generated far more traffic than they expected. Smart coffee maker broadcasts 1TB of data in 10 days After his post went viral, Nomad explained that he had worked in IT for more than 10 years and decided to look further into what had happened. Article continues after ad He found that while the coffee maker had generated 1TB of traffic, most of it stayed within his parents’ home network rather than being sent over the internet. “This is likely a bug with this unit,” he explained. “It did saturate my AP, that sucked.” In simpler terms, the coffee maker was generating so much traffic that it overwhelmed part of the home Wi-Fi setup. Hey uh, @Keurig – what the hell is a COFFEE MACHINE uploading, let me double check… ONE FUCKING TERABYTE OF DATA IN 10 DAYS!?!? Immediately unplugging that. Getting my parents a new coffee machine. pic.twitter.com/tTHMYC7hND — Nomad (@NomadsGalaxy) October 6, 2026 Nomad considered digging deeper to find out exactly what the machine was doing, but ultimately decided it wasn’t worth keeping the device connected. Article continues after ad Article continues after ad “It’s not worth keeping an IOT device connected that has the capability of bugging out and causing saturation like this did,” he said. The coffee maker belonged to his parents, with Nomad explaining that he helps them manage their internet setup remotely. “For those wondering why this is on my network, this belongs to my parents. I don’t police what they buy.
